1 # Docstrings for generated ufuncs
2 #
3 # The syntax is designed to look like the function add_newdoc is being
4 # called from numpy.lib, but in this file add_newdoc puts the
5 # docstrings in a dictionary. This dictionary is used in
6 # _generate_pyx.py to generate the docstrings for the ufuncs in
7 # scipy.special at the C level when the ufuncs are created at compile
8 # time.
9  
10 docdict: dict[str, str] = {}
11  
12  
13 def get(name):
14 return docdict.get(name)
15  
16  
17 def add_newdoc(name, doc):
18 docdict[name] = doc

85 add_newdoc("wrightomega",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
86 r"""
87 wrightomega(z, out=None)
88  
89 Wright Omega function.
90  
91 Defined as the solution to
92  
93 .. math::
94  
95 \omega + \log(\omega) = z
96  
97 where :math:`\log` is the principal branch of the complex logarithm.
98  
99 Parameters
100 ----------
101 z : array_like
102 Points at which to evaluate the Wright Omega function
103 out : ndarray, optional
104 Optional output array for the function values
105  
106 Returns
107 -------
108 omega : scalar or ndarray
109 Values of the Wright Omega function
110  
111 See Also
112 --------
113 lambertw : The Lambert W function
114  
115 Notes
116 -----
117 .. versionadded:: 0.19.0
118  
119 The function can also be defined as
120  
121 .. math::
122  
123 \omega(z) = W_{K(z)}(e^z)
124  
125 where :math:`K(z) = \lceil (\Im(z) - \pi)/(2\pi) \rceil` is the
126 unwinding number and :math:`W` is the Lambert W function.
127  
128 The implementation here is taken from [1]_.
129  
130 References
131 ----------
132 .. [1] Lawrence, Corless, and Jeffrey, "Algorithm 917: Complex
133 Double-Precision Evaluation of the Wright :math:`\omega`
134 Function." ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software,
135 2012. :doi:`10.1145/2168773.2168779`.
136  
137 Examples
138 --------
139 >>> import numpy as np
140 >>> from scipy.special import wrightomega, lambertw
141  
142 >>> wrightomega([-2, -1, 0, 1, 2])
143 array([0.12002824, 0.27846454, 0.56714329, 1. , 1.5571456 ])
144  
145 Complex input:
146  
147 >>> wrightomega(3 + 5j)
148 (1.5804428632097158+3.8213626783287937j)
149  
150 Verify that ``wrightomega(z)`` satisfies ``w + log(w) = z``:
151  
152 >>> w = -5 + 4j
153 >>> wrightomega(w + np.log(w))
154 (-5+4j)
155  
156 Verify the connection to ``lambertw``:
157  
158 >>> z = 0.5 + 3j
159 >>> wrightomega(z)
160 (0.0966015889280649+1.4937828458191993j)
161 >>> lambertw(np.exp(z))
162 (0.09660158892806493+1.4937828458191993j)
163  
164 >>> z = 0.5 + 4j
165 >>> wrightomega(z)
166 (-0.3362123489037213+2.282986001579032j)
167 >>> lambertw(np.exp(z), k=1)
168 (-0.33621234890372115+2.282986001579032j)
169 """)

  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
173 """
174 agm(a, b, out=None)
175  
176 Compute the arithmetic-geometric mean of `a` and `b`.
177  
178 Start with a_0 = a and b_0 = b and iteratively compute::
179  
180 a_{n+1} = (a_n + b_n)/2
181 b_{n+1} = sqrt(a_n*b_n)
182  
183 a_n and b_n converge to the same limit as n increases; their common
184 limit is agm(a, b).
185  
186 Parameters
187 ----------
188 a, b : array_like
189 Real values only. If the values are both negative, the result
190 is negative. If one value is negative and the other is positive,
191 `nan` is returned.
192 out : ndarray, optional
193 Optional output array for the function values
194  
195 Returns
196 -------
197 scalar or ndarray
198 The arithmetic-geometric mean of `a` and `b`.
199  
200 Examples
201 --------
202 >>> import numpy as np
203 >>> from scipy.special import agm
204 >>> a, b = 24.0, 6.0
205 >>> agm(a, b)
206 13.458171481725614
207  
208 Compare that result to the iteration:
209  
210 >>> while a != b:
211 ... a, b = (a + b)/2, np.sqrt(a*b)
212 ... print("a = %19.16f b=%19.16f" % (a, b))
213 ...
214 a = 15.0000000000000000 b=12.0000000000000000
215 a = 13.5000000000000000 b=13.4164078649987388
216 a = 13.4582039324993694 b=13.4581390309909850
217 a = 13.4581714817451772 b=13.4581714817060547
218 a = 13.4581714817256159 b=13.4581714817256159
219  
220 When array-like arguments are given, broadcasting applies:
221  
222 >>> a = np.array([[1.5], [3], [6]]) # a has shape (3, 1).
223 >>> b = np.array([6, 12, 24, 48]) # b has shape (4,).
224 >>> agm(a, b)
225 array([[ 3.36454287, 5.42363427, 9.05798751, 15.53650756],
226 [ 4.37037309, 6.72908574, 10.84726853, 18.11597502],
227 [ 6. , 8.74074619, 13.45817148, 21.69453707]])
228 """)

230 add_newdoc("airy",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
231 r"""
232 airy(z, out=None)
233  
234 Airy functions and their derivatives.
235  
236 Parameters
237 ----------
238 z : array_like
239 Real or complex argument.
240 out : tuple of ndarray, optional
241 Optional output arrays for the function values
242  
243 Returns
244 -------
245 Ai, Aip, Bi, Bip : 4-tuple of scalar or ndarray
246 Airy functions Ai and Bi, and their derivatives Aip and Bip.
247  
248 See Also
249 --------
250 airye : exponentially scaled Airy functions.
251  
252 Notes
253 -----
254 The Airy functions Ai and Bi are two independent solutions of
255  
256 .. math:: y''(x) = x y(x).
257  
258 For real `z` in [-10, 10], the computation is carried out by calling
259 the Cephes [1]_ `airy` routine, which uses power series summation
260 for small `z` and rational minimax approximations for large `z`.
261  
262 Outside this range, the AMOS [2]_ `zairy` and `zbiry` routines are
263 employed. They are computed using power series for :math:`|z| < 1` and
264 the following relations to modified Bessel functions for larger `z`
265 (where :math:`t \equiv 2 z^{3/2}/3`):
266  
267 .. math::
268  
269 Ai(z) = \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{3}} K_{1/3}(t)
270  
271 Ai'(z) = -\frac{z}{\pi \sqrt{3}} K_{2/3}(t)
272  
273 Bi(z) = \sqrt{\frac{z}{3}} \left(I_{-1/3}(t) + I_{1/3}(t) \right)
274  
275 Bi'(z) = \frac{z}{\sqrt{3}} \left(I_{-2/3}(t) + I_{2/3}(t)\right)
276  
277 References
278 ----------
279 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
280 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
281 .. [2] Donald E. Amos, "AMOS, A Portable Package for Bessel Functions
282 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",
283 http://netlib.org/amos/
284  
285 Examples
286 --------
287 Compute the Airy functions on the interval [-15, 5].
288  
289 >>> import numpy as np
290 >>> from scipy import special
291 >>> x = np.linspace(-15, 5, 201)
292 >>> ai, aip, bi, bip = special.airy(x)
293  
294 Plot Ai(x) and Bi(x).
295  
296 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
297 >>> plt.plot(x, ai, 'r', label='Ai(x)')
298 >>> plt.plot(x, bi, 'b--', label='Bi(x)')
299 >>> plt.ylim(-0.5, 1.0)
300 >>> plt.grid()
301 >>> plt.legend(loc='upper left')
302 >>> plt.show()
303  
304 """)
305  
306 add_newdoc("airye",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
307 """
308 airye(z, out=None)
309  
310 Exponentially scaled Airy functions and their derivatives.
311  
312 Scaling::
313  
314 eAi = Ai * exp(2.0/3.0*z*sqrt(z))
315 eAip = Aip * exp(2.0/3.0*z*sqrt(z))
316 eBi = Bi * exp(-abs(2.0/3.0*(z*sqrt(z)).real))
317 eBip = Bip * exp(-abs(2.0/3.0*(z*sqrt(z)).real))
318  
319 Parameters
320 ----------
321 z : array_like
322 Real or complex argument.
323 out : tuple of ndarray, optional
324 Optional output arrays for the function values
325  
326 Returns
327 -------
328 eAi, eAip, eBi, eBip : 4-tuple of scalar or ndarray
329 Exponentially scaled Airy functions eAi and eBi, and their derivatives
330 eAip and eBip
331  
332 See Also
333 --------
334 airy
335  
336 Notes
337 -----
338 Wrapper for the AMOS [1]_ routines `zairy` and `zbiry`.
339  
340 References
341 ----------
342 .. [1] Donald E. Amos, "AMOS, A Portable Package for Bessel Functions
343 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",
344 http://netlib.org/amos/
345  
346 Examples
347 --------
348 We can compute exponentially scaled Airy functions and their derivatives:
349  
350 >>> import numpy as np
351 >>> from scipy.special import airye
352 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
353 >>> z = np.linspace(0, 50, 500)
354 >>> eAi, eAip, eBi, eBip = airye(z)
355 >>> f, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)
356 >>> for ind, data in enumerate([[eAi, eAip, ["eAi", "eAip"]],
357 ... [eBi, eBip, ["eBi", "eBip"]]]):
358 ... ax[ind].plot(z, data[0], "-r", z, data[1], "-b")
359 ... ax[ind].legend(data[2])
360 ... ax[ind].grid(True)
361 >>> plt.show()
362  
363 We can compute these using usual non-scaled Airy functions by:
364  
365 >>> from scipy.special import airy
366 >>> Ai, Aip, Bi, Bip = airy(z)
367 >>> np.allclose(eAi, Ai * np.exp(2.0 / 3.0 * z * np.sqrt(z)))
368 True
369 >>> np.allclose(eAip, Aip * np.exp(2.0 / 3.0 * z * np.sqrt(z)))
370 True
  • E501 Line too long (80 > 79 characters)
371 >>> np.allclose(eBi, Bi * np.exp(-abs(np.real(2.0 / 3.0 * z * np.sqrt(z)))))
372 True
  • E501 Line too long (82 > 79 characters)
373 >>> np.allclose(eBip, Bip * np.exp(-abs(np.real(2.0 / 3.0 * z * np.sqrt(z)))))
374 True
375  
376 Comparing non-scaled and exponentially scaled ones, the usual non-scaled
377 function quickly underflows for large values, whereas the exponentially
378 scaled function does not.
379  
380 >>> airy(200)
381 (0.0, 0.0, nan, nan)
382 >>> airye(200)
  • E501 Line too long (87 > 79 characters)
383 (0.07501041684381093, -1.0609012305109042, 0.15003188417418148, 2.1215836725571093)
384  
385 """)

388 r"""
389 bdtr(k, n, p, out=None)
390  
391 Binomial distribution cumulative distribution function.
392  
393 Sum of the terms 0 through `floor(k)` of the Binomial probability density.
394  
395 .. math::
396 \mathrm{bdtr}(k, n, p) =
397 \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k \rfloor} {{n}\choose{j}} p^j (1-p)^{n-j}
398  
399 Parameters
400 ----------
401 k : array_like
402 Number of successes (double), rounded down to the nearest integer.
403 n : array_like
404 Number of events (int).
405 p : array_like
406 Probability of success in a single event (float).
407 out : ndarray, optional
408 Optional output array for the function values
409  
410 Returns
411 -------
412 y : scalar or ndarray
  • E501 Line too long (83 > 79 characters)
413 Probability of `floor(k)` or fewer successes in `n` independent events with
414 success probabilities of `p`.
415  
416 Notes
417 -----
418 The terms are not summed directly; instead the regularized incomplete beta
419 function is employed, according to the formula,
420  
421 .. math::
422 \mathrm{bdtr}(k, n, p) =
423 I_{1 - p}(n - \lfloor k \rfloor, \lfloor k \rfloor + 1).
424  
425 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `bdtr`.
426  
427 References
428 ----------
429 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
430 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
431  
432 """)

487 r"""
488 bdtri(k, n, y, out=None)
489  
490 Inverse function to `bdtr` with respect to `p`.
491  
492 Finds the event probability `p` such that the sum of the terms 0 through
493 `k` of the binomial probability density is equal to the given cumulative
494 probability `y`.
495  
496 Parameters
497 ----------
498 k : array_like
499 Number of successes (float), rounded down to the nearest integer.
500 n : array_like
501 Number of events (float)
502 y : array_like
503 Cumulative probability (probability of `k` or fewer successes in `n`
504 events).
505 out : ndarray, optional
506 Optional output array for the function values
507  
508 Returns
509 -------
510 p : scalar or ndarray
511 The event probability such that `bdtr(\lfloor k \rfloor, n, p) = y`.
512  
513 See Also
514 --------
515 bdtr
516 betaincinv
517  
518 Notes
519 -----
520 The computation is carried out using the inverse beta integral function
521 and the relation,::
522  
523 1 - p = betaincinv(n - k, k + 1, y).
524  
525 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `bdtri`.
526  
527 References
528 ----------
529 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
530 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/

534 """
535 bdtrik(y, n, p, out=None)
536  
537 Inverse function to `bdtr` with respect to `k`.
538  
539 Finds the number of successes `k` such that the sum of the terms 0 through
540 `k` of the Binomial probability density for `n` events with probability
541 `p` is equal to the given cumulative probability `y`.
542  
543 Parameters
544 ----------
545 y : array_like
546 Cumulative probability (probability of `k` or fewer successes in `n`
547 events).
548 n : array_like
549 Number of events (float).
550 p : array_like
551 Success probability (float).
552 out : ndarray, optional
553 Optional output array for the function values
554  
555 Returns
556 -------
557 k : scalar or ndarray
558 The number of successes `k` such that `bdtr(k, n, p) = y`.
559  
560 See Also
561 --------
562 bdtr
563  
564 Notes
565 -----
566 Formula 26.5.24 of [1]_ is used to reduce the binomial distribution to the
567 cumulative incomplete beta distribution.
568  
569 Computation of `k` involves a search for a value that produces the desired
570 value of `y`. The search relies on the monotonicity of `y` with `k`.
571  
572 Wrapper for the CDFLIB [2]_ Fortran routine `cdfbin`.
573  
574 References
575 ----------
576 .. [1] Milton Abramowitz and Irene A. Stegun, eds.
577 Handbook of Mathematical Functions with Formulas,
578 Graphs, and Mathematical Tables. New York: Dover, 1972.
579 .. [2] Barry Brown, James Lovato, and Kathy Russell,
580 CDFLIB: Library of Fortran Routines for Cumulative Distribution
581 Functions, Inverses, and Other Parameters.
582  
583 """)

743 add_newdoc(
744 "betainc",
745 r"""
746 betainc(a, b, x, out=None)
747  
748 Regularized incomplete beta function.
749  
750 Computes the regularized incomplete beta function, defined as [1]_:
751  
752 .. math::
753  
754 I_x(a, b) = \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \int_0^x
755 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}dt,
756  
757 for :math:`0 \leq x \leq 1`.
758  
759 This function is the cumulative distribution function for the beta
760 distribution; its range is [0, 1].
761  
762 Parameters
763 ----------
764 a, b : array_like
765 Positive, real-valued parameters
766 x : array_like
767 Real-valued such that :math:`0 \leq x \leq 1`,
768 the upper limit of integration
769 out : ndarray, optional
770 Optional output array for the function values
771  
772 Returns
773 -------
774 scalar or ndarray
775 Value of the regularized incomplete beta function
776  
777 See Also
778 --------
779 beta : beta function
780 betaincinv : inverse of the regularized incomplete beta function
781 betaincc : complement of the regularized incomplete beta function
782 scipy.stats.beta : beta distribution
783  
784 Notes
785 -----
786 The term *regularized* in the name of this function refers to the
787 scaling of the function by the gamma function terms shown in the
788 formula. When not qualified as *regularized*, the name *incomplete
789 beta function* often refers to just the integral expression,
790 without the gamma terms. One can use the function `beta` from
791 `scipy.special` to get this "nonregularized" incomplete beta
792 function by multiplying the result of ``betainc(a, b, x)`` by
793 ``beta(a, b)``.
794  
795 ``betainc(a, b, x)`` is treated as a two parameter family of functions
796 of a single variable `x`, rather than as a function of three variables.
797 This impacts only the limiting cases ``a = 0``, ``b = 0``, ``a = inf``,
798 ``b = inf``.
799  
800 In general
801  
802 .. math::
803  
804 \lim_{(a, b) \rightarrow (a_0, b_0)} \mathrm{betainc}(a, b, x)
805  
806 is treated as a pointwise limit in ``x``. Thus for example,
807 ``betainc(0, b, 0)`` equals ``0`` for ``b > 0``, although it would be
  • E501 Line too long (81 > 79 characters)
808 indeterminate when considering the simultaneous limit ``(a, x) -> (0+, 0+)``.
809  
810 This function wraps the ``ibeta`` routine from the
811 Boost Math C++ library [2]_.
812  
813 References
814 ----------
815 .. [1] NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
816 https://dlmf.nist.gov/8.17
817 .. [2] The Boost Developers. "Boost C++ Libraries". https://www.boost.org/.
818  
819 Examples
820 --------
821  
822 Let :math:`B(a, b)` be the `beta` function.
823  
824 >>> import scipy.special as sc
825  
826 The coefficient in terms of `gamma` is equal to
827 :math:`1/B(a, b)`. Also, when :math:`x=1`
828 the integral is equal to :math:`B(a, b)`.
829 Therefore, :math:`I_{x=1}(a, b) = 1` for any :math:`a, b`.
830  
831 >>> sc.betainc(0.2, 3.5, 1.0)
832 1.0
833  
834 It satisfies
835 :math:`I_x(a, b) = x^a F(a, 1-b, a+1, x)/ (aB(a, b))`,
836 where :math:`F` is the hypergeometric function `hyp2f1`:
837  
838 >>> a, b, x = 1.4, 3.1, 0.5
839 >>> x**a * sc.hyp2f1(a, 1 - b, a + 1, x)/(a * sc.beta(a, b))
840 0.8148904036225295
841 >>> sc.betainc(a, b, x)
842 0.8148904036225296
843  
844 This functions satisfies the relationship
845 :math:`I_x(a, b) = 1 - I_{1-x}(b, a)`:
846  
847 >>> sc.betainc(2.2, 3.1, 0.4)
848 0.49339638807619446
849 >>> 1 - sc.betainc(3.1, 2.2, 1 - 0.4)
850 0.49339638807619446
851  
852 """)
853

856 "betaincc",
857 r"""
858 betaincc(a, b, x, out=None)
859  
860 Complement of the regularized incomplete beta function.
861  
862 Computes the complement of the regularized incomplete beta function,
863 defined as [1]_:
864  
865 .. math::
866  
867 \bar{I}_x(a, b) = 1 - I_x(a, b)
868 = 1 - \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \int_0^x
869 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}dt,
870  
871 for :math:`0 \leq x \leq 1`.
872  
873 Parameters
874 ----------
875 a, b : array_like
876 Positive, real-valued parameters
877 x : array_like
878 Real-valued such that :math:`0 \leq x \leq 1`,
879 the upper limit of integration
880 out : ndarray, optional
881 Optional output array for the function values
882  
883 Returns
884 -------
885 scalar or ndarray
886 Value of the regularized incomplete beta function
887  
888 See Also
889 --------
890 betainc : regularized incomplete beta function
891 betaincinv : inverse of the regularized incomplete beta function
892 betainccinv :
893 inverse of the complement of the regularized incomplete beta function
894 beta : beta function
895 scipy.stats.beta : beta distribution
896  
897 Notes
898 -----
899 .. versionadded:: 1.11.0
900  
901 Like `betainc`, ``betaincc(a, b, x)`` is treated as a two parameter
902 family of functions of a single variable `x`, rather than as a function of
903 three variables. See the `betainc` docstring for more info on how this
904 impacts limiting cases.
905  
906 This function wraps the ``ibetac`` routine from the
907 Boost Math C++ library [2]_.
908  
909 References
910 ----------
911 .. [1] NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
912 https://dlmf.nist.gov/8.17
913 .. [2] The Boost Developers. "Boost C++ Libraries". https://www.boost.org/.
914  
915 Examples
916 --------
917 >>> from scipy.special import betaincc, betainc
918  
919 The naive calculation ``1 - betainc(a, b, x)`` loses precision when
920 the values of ``betainc(a, b, x)`` are close to 1:
921  
922 >>> 1 - betainc(0.5, 8, [0.9, 0.99, 0.999])
923 array([2.0574632e-09, 0.0000000e+00, 0.0000000e+00])
924  
925 By using ``betaincc``, we get the correct values:
926  
927 >>> betaincc(0.5, 8, [0.9, 0.99, 0.999])

1069 boxcox(x, lmbda, out=None)
1070  
1071 Compute the Box-Cox transformation.
1072  
1073 The Box-Cox transformation is::
1074  
1075 y = (x**lmbda - 1) / lmbda if lmbda != 0
1076 log(x) if lmbda == 0
1077  
1078 Returns `nan` if ``x < 0``.
1079 Returns `-inf` if ``x == 0`` and ``lmbda < 0``.
1080

1082 ----------
1083 x : array_like
1084 Data to be transformed.
1085 lmbda : array_like
1086 Power parameter of the Box-Cox transform.
1087 out : ndarray, optional
1088 Optional output array for the function values
1089  
1090 Returns
1091 -------
1092 y : scalar or ndarray
1093 Transformed data.
1094  
1095 Notes
1096 -----
1097  
1098 .. versionadded:: 0.14.0
1099  
1100 Examples
1101 --------
1102 >>> from scipy.special import boxcox
1103 >>> boxcox([1, 4, 10], 2.5)
1104 array([ 0. , 12.4 , 126.09110641])
1105 >>> boxcox(2, [0, 1, 2])
1106 array([ 0.69314718, 1. , 1.5 ])

1228 r"""
1229 chdtr(v, x, out=None)
1230  
1231 Chi square cumulative distribution function.
1232  
1233 Returns the area under the left tail (from 0 to `x`) of the Chi
1234 square probability density function with `v` degrees of freedom:
1235  
1236 .. math::
1237  
1238 \frac{1}{2^{v/2} \Gamma(v/2)} \int_0^x t^{v/2 - 1} e^{-t/2} dt
1239  
1240 Here :math:`\Gamma` is the Gamma function; see `gamma`. This
1241 integral can be expressed in terms of the regularized lower
1242 incomplete gamma function `gammainc` as
1243 ``gammainc(v / 2, x / 2)``. [1]_
1244  
1245 Parameters
1246 ----------
1247 v : array_like
1248 Degrees of freedom.
1249 x : array_like
1250 Upper bound of the integral.
1251 out : ndarray, optional
1252 Optional output array for the function results.
1253  
1254 Returns
1255 -------
1256 scalar or ndarray
1257 Values of the cumulative distribution function.
1258  
1259 See Also
1260 --------
1261 chdtrc, chdtri, chdtriv, gammainc
1262  
1263 References
1264 ----------
1265 .. [1] Chi-Square distribution,
1266 https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3666.htm
1267  
1268 Examples
1269 --------
1270 >>> import numpy as np
1271 >>> import scipy.special as sc
1272  
1273 It can be expressed in terms of the regularized lower incomplete
1274 gamma function.
1275  
1276 >>> v = 1
1277 >>> x = np.arange(4)
1278 >>> sc.chdtr(v, x)
1279 array([0. , 0.68268949, 0.84270079, 0.91673548])
1280 >>> sc.gammainc(v / 2, x / 2)
1281 array([0. , 0.68268949, 0.84270079, 0.91673548])
1282  
1283 """)

1439 r"""
1440 chndtr(x, df, nc, out=None)
1441  
1442 Non-central chi square cumulative distribution function
1443  
1444 The cumulative distribution function is given by:
1445  
1446 .. math::
1447  
1448 P(\chi^{\prime 2} \vert \nu, \lambda) =\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}
1449 e^{-\lambda /2}
1450 \frac{(\lambda /2)^j}{j!} P(\chi^{\prime 2} \vert \nu + 2j),
1451  
1452 where :math:`\nu > 0` is the degrees of freedom (``df``) and
1453 :math:`\lambda \geq 0` is the non-centrality parameter (``nc``).
1454  
1455 Parameters
1456 ----------
1457 x : array_like
1458 Upper bound of the integral; must satisfy ``x >= 0``
1459 df : array_like
1460 Degrees of freedom; must satisfy ``df > 0``
1461 nc : array_like
1462 Non-centrality parameter; must satisfy ``nc >= 0``
1463 out : ndarray, optional
1464 Optional output array for the function results
1465  
1466 Returns
1467 -------
1468 x : scalar or ndarray
1469 Value of the non-central chi square cumulative distribution function.
1470  
1471 See Also
1472 --------
1473 chndtrix, chndtridf, chndtrinc
1474  
1475 """)

1573 "elliprc",
1574 r"""
1575 elliprc(x, y, out=None)
1576  
1577 Degenerate symmetric elliptic integral.
1578  
1579 The function RC is defined as [1]_
1580  
1581 .. math::
1582  
1583 R_{\mathrm{C}}(x, y) =
1584 \frac{1}{2} \int_0^{+\infty} (t + x)^{-1/2} (t + y)^{-1} dt
1585 = R_{\mathrm{F}}(x, y, y)
1586  
1587 Parameters
1588 ----------
1589 x, y : array_like
1590 Real or complex input parameters. `x` can be any number in the
1591 complex plane cut along the negative real axis. `y` must be non-zero.
1592 out : ndarray, optional
1593 Optional output array for the function values
1594  
1595 Returns
1596 -------
1597 R : scalar or ndarray
1598 Value of the integral. If `y` is real and negative, the Cauchy
1599 principal value is returned. If both of `x` and `y` are real, the
1600 return value is real. Otherwise, the return value is complex.
1601  
1602 See Also
1603 --------
1604 elliprf : Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the first kind.
1605 elliprd : Symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
1606 elliprg : Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
1607 elliprj : Symmetric elliptic integral of the third kind.
1608  
1609 Notes
1610 -----
1611 RC is a degenerate case of the symmetric integral RF: ``elliprc(x, y) ==
1612 elliprf(x, y, y)``. It is an elementary function rather than an elliptic
1613 integral.
1614  
1615 The code implements Carlson's algorithm based on the duplication theorems
1616 and series expansion up to the 7th order. [2]_
1617  
1618 .. versionadded:: 1.8.0
1619  
1620 References
1621 ----------
1622 .. [1] B. C. Carlson, ed., Chapter 19 in "Digital Library of Mathematical
1623 Functions," NIST, US Dept. of Commerce.
1624 https://dlmf.nist.gov/19.16.E6
1625 .. [2] B. C. Carlson, "Numerical computation of real or complex elliptic
1626 integrals," Numer. Algorithm, vol. 10, no. 1, pp. 13-26, 1995.
1627 https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9409227
1628 https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02198293
1629  
1630 Examples
1631 --------
1632 Basic homogeneity property:
1633  
1634 >>> import numpy as np
1635 >>> from scipy.special import elliprc
1636  
1637 >>> x = 1.2 + 3.4j
1638 >>> y = 5.
1639 >>> scale = 0.3 + 0.4j
1640 >>> elliprc(scale*x, scale*y)
1641 (0.5484493976710874-0.4169557678995833j)
1642  
1643 >>> elliprc(x, y)/np.sqrt(scale)
1644 (0.5484493976710874-0.41695576789958333j)
1645  
1646 When the two arguments coincide, the integral is particularly
1647 simple:
1648  
1649 >>> x = 1.2 + 3.4j
1650 >>> elliprc(x, x)
1651 (0.4299173120614631-0.3041729818745595j)
1652  
1653 >>> 1/np.sqrt(x)
1654 (0.4299173120614631-0.30417298187455954j)
1655  
1656 Another simple case: the first argument vanishes:
1657  
1658 >>> y = 1.2 + 3.4j
1659 >>> elliprc(0, y)
1660 (0.6753125346116815-0.47779380263880866j)
1661  
1662 >>> np.pi/2/np.sqrt(y)
1663 (0.6753125346116815-0.4777938026388088j)
1664  
1665 When `x` and `y` are both positive, we can express
1666 :math:`R_C(x,y)` in terms of more elementary functions. For the
1667 case :math:`0 \le x < y`,
1668  
1669 >>> x = 3.2
1670 >>> y = 6.
1671 >>> elliprc(x, y)
1672 0.44942991498453444
1673  
1674 >>> np.arctan(np.sqrt((y-x)/x))/np.sqrt(y-x)
1675 0.44942991498453433
1676  
1677 And for the case :math:`0 \le y < x`,
1678  
1679 >>> x = 6.
1680 >>> y = 3.2
1681 >>> elliprc(x,y)
1682 0.4989837501576147
1683  
1684 >>> np.log((np.sqrt(x)+np.sqrt(x-y))/np.sqrt(y))/np.sqrt(x-y)
1685 0.49898375015761476
1686  
1687 """)
1688

1691 r"""
1692 elliprd(x, y, z, out=None)
1693  
1694 Symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
1695  
1696 The function RD is defined as [1]_
1697  
1698 .. math::
1699  
1700 R_{\mathrm{D}}(x, y, z) =
1701 \frac{3}{2} \int_0^{+\infty} [(t + x) (t + y)]^{-1/2} (t + z)^{-3/2}
1702 dt
1703  
1704 Parameters
1705 ----------
1706 x, y, z : array_like
1707 Real or complex input parameters. `x` or `y` can be any number in the
1708 complex plane cut along the negative real axis, but at most one of them
1709 can be zero, while `z` must be non-zero.
1710 out : ndarray, optional
1711 Optional output array for the function values
1712  
1713 Returns
1714 -------
1715 R : scalar or ndarray
1716 Value of the integral. If all of `x`, `y`, and `z` are real, the
1717 return value is real. Otherwise, the return value is complex.
1718  
1719 See Also
1720 --------
1721 elliprc : Degenerate symmetric elliptic integral.
1722 elliprf : Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the first kind.
1723 elliprg : Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
1724 elliprj : Symmetric elliptic integral of the third kind.
1725  
1726 Notes
1727 -----
1728 RD is a degenerate case of the elliptic integral RJ: ``elliprd(x, y, z) ==
1729 elliprj(x, y, z, z)``.
1730  
1731 The code implements Carlson's algorithm based on the duplication theorems
1732 and series expansion up to the 7th order. [2]_
1733  
1734 .. versionadded:: 1.8.0
1735  
1736 References
1737 ----------
1738 .. [1] B. C. Carlson, ed., Chapter 19 in "Digital Library of Mathematical
1739 Functions," NIST, US Dept. of Commerce.
1740 https://dlmf.nist.gov/19.16.E5
1741 .. [2] B. C. Carlson, "Numerical computation of real or complex elliptic
1742 integrals," Numer. Algorithm, vol. 10, no. 1, pp. 13-26, 1995.
1743 https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9409227
1744 https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02198293
1745  
1746 Examples
1747 --------
1748 Basic homogeneity property:
1749  
1750 >>> import numpy as np
1751 >>> from scipy.special import elliprd
1752  
1753 >>> x = 1.2 + 3.4j
1754 >>> y = 5.
1755 >>> z = 6.
1756 >>> scale = 0.3 + 0.4j
1757 >>> elliprd(scale*x, scale*y, scale*z)
1758 (-0.03703043835680379-0.24500934665683802j)
1759  
1760 >>> elliprd(x, y, z)*np.power(scale, -1.5)
1761 (-0.0370304383568038-0.24500934665683805j)
1762  
1763 All three arguments coincide:
1764  
1765 >>> x = 1.2 + 3.4j
1766 >>> elliprd(x, x, x)
1767 (-0.03986825876151896-0.14051741840449586j)
1768  
1769 >>> np.power(x, -1.5)
1770 (-0.03986825876151894-0.14051741840449583j)
1771  
1772 The so-called "second lemniscate constant":
1773  
1774 >>> elliprd(0, 2, 1)/3
1775 0.5990701173677961
1776  
1777 >>> from scipy.special import gamma
1778 >>> gamma(0.75)**2/np.sqrt(2*np.pi)
1779 0.5990701173677959
1780  
1781 """)

1785 r"""
1786 elliprf(x, y, z, out=None)
1787  
1788 Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the first kind.
1789  
1790 The function RF is defined as [1]_
1791  
1792 .. math::
1793  
1794 R_{\mathrm{F}}(x, y, z) =
1795 \frac{1}{2} \int_0^{+\infty} [(t + x) (t + y) (t + z)]^{-1/2} dt
1796  
1797 Parameters
1798 ----------
1799 x, y, z : array_like
1800 Real or complex input parameters. `x`, `y`, or `z` can be any number in
1801 the complex plane cut along the negative real axis, but at most one of
1802 them can be zero.
1803 out : ndarray, optional
1804 Optional output array for the function values
1805  
1806 Returns
1807 -------
1808 R : scalar or ndarray
1809 Value of the integral. If all of `x`, `y`, and `z` are real, the return
1810 value is real. Otherwise, the return value is complex.
1811  
1812 See Also
1813 --------
1814 elliprc : Degenerate symmetric integral.
1815 elliprd : Symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
1816 elliprg : Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
1817 elliprj : Symmetric elliptic integral of the third kind.
1818  
1819 Notes
1820 -----
1821 The code implements Carlson's algorithm based on the duplication theorems
1822 and series expansion up to the 7th order (cf.:
1823 https://dlmf.nist.gov/19.36.i) and the AGM algorithm for the complete
1824 integral. [2]_
1825  
1826 .. versionadded:: 1.8.0
1827  
1828 References
1829 ----------
1830 .. [1] B. C. Carlson, ed., Chapter 19 in "Digital Library of Mathematical
1831 Functions," NIST, US Dept. of Commerce.
1832 https://dlmf.nist.gov/19.16.E1
1833 .. [2] B. C. Carlson, "Numerical computation of real or complex elliptic
1834 integrals," Numer. Algorithm, vol. 10, no. 1, pp. 13-26, 1995.
1835 https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9409227
1836 https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02198293
1837  
1838 Examples
1839 --------
1840 Basic homogeneity property:
1841  
1842 >>> import numpy as np
1843 >>> from scipy.special import elliprf
1844  
1845 >>> x = 1.2 + 3.4j
1846 >>> y = 5.
1847 >>> z = 6.
1848 >>> scale = 0.3 + 0.4j
1849 >>> elliprf(scale*x, scale*y, scale*z)
1850 (0.5328051227278146-0.4008623567957094j)
1851  
1852 >>> elliprf(x, y, z)/np.sqrt(scale)
1853 (0.5328051227278147-0.4008623567957095j)
1854  
1855 All three arguments coincide:
1856  
1857 >>> x = 1.2 + 3.4j
1858 >>> elliprf(x, x, x)
1859 (0.42991731206146316-0.30417298187455954j)
1860  
1861 >>> 1/np.sqrt(x)
1862 (0.4299173120614631-0.30417298187455954j)
1863  
1864 The so-called "first lemniscate constant":
1865  
1866 >>> elliprf(0, 1, 2)
1867 1.3110287771460598
1868  
1869 >>> from scipy.special import gamma
1870 >>> gamma(0.25)**2/(4*np.sqrt(2*np.pi))

1876 "elliprg",
1877 r"""
1878 elliprg(x, y, z, out=None)
1879  
1880 Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
1881  
1882 The function RG is defined as [1]_
1883  
1884 .. math::
1885  
1886 R_{\mathrm{G}}(x, y, z) =
1887 \frac{1}{4} \int_0^{+\infty} [(t + x) (t + y) (t + z)]^{-1/2}
1888 \left(\frac{x}{t + x} + \frac{y}{t + y} + \frac{z}{t + z}\right) t
1889 dt
1890  
1891 Parameters
1892 ----------
1893 x, y, z : array_like
1894 Real or complex input parameters. `x`, `y`, or `z` can be any number in
1895 the complex plane cut along the negative real axis.
1896 out : ndarray, optional
1897 Optional output array for the function values
1898  
1899 Returns
1900 -------
1901 R : scalar or ndarray
1902 Value of the integral. If all of `x`, `y`, and `z` are real, the return
1903 value is real. Otherwise, the return value is complex.
1904  
1905 See Also
1906 --------
1907 elliprc : Degenerate symmetric integral.
1908 elliprd : Symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
1909 elliprf : Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the first kind.
1910 elliprj : Symmetric elliptic integral of the third kind.
1911  
1912 Notes
1913 -----
1914 The implementation uses the relation [1]_
1915  
1916 .. math::
1917  
1918 2 R_{\mathrm{G}}(x, y, z) =
1919 z R_{\mathrm{F}}(x, y, z) -
1920 \frac{1}{3} (x - z) (y - z) R_{\mathrm{D}}(x, y, z) +
1921 \sqrt{\frac{x y}{z}}
1922  
1923 and the symmetry of `x`, `y`, `z` when at least one non-zero parameter can
1924 be chosen as the pivot. When one of the arguments is close to zero, the AGM
1925 method is applied instead. Other special cases are computed following Ref.
1926 [2]_
1927  
1928 .. versionadded:: 1.8.0
1929  
1930 References
1931 ----------
1932 .. [1] B. C. Carlson, "Numerical computation of real or complex elliptic
1933 integrals," Numer. Algorithm, vol. 10, no. 1, pp. 13-26, 1995.
1934 https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9409227
1935 https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02198293
1936 .. [2] B. C. Carlson, ed., Chapter 19 in "Digital Library of Mathematical
1937 Functions," NIST, US Dept. of Commerce.
1938 https://dlmf.nist.gov/19.16.E1
1939 https://dlmf.nist.gov/19.20.ii
1940  
1941 Examples
1942 --------
1943 Basic homogeneity property:
1944  
1945 >>> import numpy as np
1946 >>> from scipy.special import elliprg
1947  
1948 >>> x = 1.2 + 3.4j
1949 >>> y = 5.
1950 >>> z = 6.
1951 >>> scale = 0.3 + 0.4j
1952 >>> elliprg(scale*x, scale*y, scale*z)
1953 (1.195936862005246+0.8470988320464167j)
1954  
1955 >>> elliprg(x, y, z)*np.sqrt(scale)
1956 (1.195936862005246+0.8470988320464165j)
1957  
1958 Simplifications:
1959  
1960 >>> elliprg(0, y, y)
1961 1.756203682760182
1962  
1963 >>> 0.25*np.pi*np.sqrt(y)
1964 1.7562036827601817
1965  
1966 >>> elliprg(0, 0, z)
1967 1.224744871391589
1968  
1969 >>> 0.5*np.sqrt(z)
1970 1.224744871391589
1971  
1972 The surface area of a triaxial ellipsoid with semiaxes ``a``, ``b``, and
1973 ``c`` is given by
1974  
1975 .. math::
1976  
1977 S = 4 \pi a b c R_{\mathrm{G}}(1 / a^2, 1 / b^2, 1 / c^2).
1978  
1979 >>> def ellipsoid_area(a, b, c):
1980 ... r = 4.0 * np.pi * a * b * c
1981 ... return r * elliprg(1.0 / (a * a), 1.0 / (b * b), 1.0 / (c * c))
1982 >>> print(ellipsoid_area(1, 3, 5))
1983 108.62688289491807
1984 """)

1987 "elliprj",
1988 r"""
1989 elliprj(x, y, z, p, out=None)
1990  
1991 Symmetric elliptic integral of the third kind.
1992  
1993 The function RJ is defined as [1]_
1994  
1995 .. math::
1996  
1997 R_{\mathrm{J}}(x, y, z, p) =
1998 \frac{3}{2} \int_0^{+\infty} [(t + x) (t + y) (t + z)]^{-1/2}
1999 (t + p)^{-1} dt
2000  
2001 .. warning::
2002 This function should be considered experimental when the inputs are
2003 unbalanced. Check correctness with another independent implementation.
2004  
2005 Parameters
2006 ----------
2007 x, y, z, p : array_like
2008 Real or complex input parameters. `x`, `y`, or `z` are numbers in
2009 the complex plane cut along the negative real axis (subject to further
2010 constraints, see Notes), and at most one of them can be zero. `p` must
2011 be non-zero.
2012 out : ndarray, optional
2013 Optional output array for the function values
2014  
2015 Returns
2016 -------
2017 R : scalar or ndarray
2018 Value of the integral. If all of `x`, `y`, `z`, and `p` are real, the
2019 return value is real. Otherwise, the return value is complex.
2020  
2021 If `p` is real and negative, while `x`, `y`, and `z` are real,
2022 non-negative, and at most one of them is zero, the Cauchy principal
2023 value is returned. [1]_ [2]_
2024  
2025 See Also
2026 --------
2027 elliprc : Degenerate symmetric integral.
2028 elliprd : Symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
2029 elliprf : Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the first kind.
2030 elliprg : Completely-symmetric elliptic integral of the second kind.
2031  
2032 Notes
2033 -----
2034 The code implements Carlson's algorithm based on the duplication theorems
2035 and series expansion up to the 7th order. [3]_ The algorithm is slightly
2036 different from its earlier incarnation as it appears in [1]_, in that the
2037 call to `elliprc` (or ``atan``/``atanh``, see [4]_) is no longer needed in
2038 the inner loop. Asymptotic approximations are used where arguments differ
2039 widely in the order of magnitude. [5]_
2040  
2041 The input values are subject to certain sufficient but not necessary
2042 constraints when input arguments are complex. Notably, ``x``, ``y``, and
2043 ``z`` must have non-negative real parts, unless two of them are
2044 non-negative and complex-conjugates to each other while the other is a real
2045 non-negative number. [1]_ If the inputs do not satisfy the sufficient
2046 condition described in Ref. [1]_ they are rejected outright with the output
2047 set to NaN.
2048  
2049 In the case where one of ``x``, ``y``, and ``z`` is equal to ``p``, the
2050 function ``elliprd`` should be preferred because of its less restrictive
2051 domain.
2052  
2053 .. versionadded:: 1.8.0
2054  
2055 References
2056 ----------
2057 .. [1] B. C. Carlson, "Numerical computation of real or complex elliptic
2058 integrals," Numer. Algorithm, vol. 10, no. 1, pp. 13-26, 1995.
2059 https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9409227
2060 https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02198293
2061 .. [2] B. C. Carlson, ed., Chapter 19 in "Digital Library of Mathematical
2062 Functions," NIST, US Dept. of Commerce.
2063 https://dlmf.nist.gov/19.20.iii
2064 .. [3] B. C. Carlson, J. FitzSimmons, "Reduction Theorems for Elliptic
2065 Integrands with the Square Root of Two Quadratic Factors," J.
2066 Comput. Appl. Math., vol. 118, nos. 1-2, pp. 71-85, 2000.
2067 https://doi.org/10.1016/S0377-0427(00)00282-X
2068 .. [4] F. Johansson, "Numerical Evaluation of Elliptic Functions, Elliptic
2069 Integrals and Modular Forms," in J. Blumlein, C. Schneider, P.
2070 Paule, eds., "Elliptic Integrals, Elliptic Functions and Modular
2071 Forms in Quantum Field Theory," pp. 269-293, 2019 (Cham,
2072 Switzerland: Springer Nature Switzerland)
2073 https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.06725
2074 https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-04480-0
2075 .. [5] B. C. Carlson, J. L. Gustafson, "Asymptotic Approximations for
2076 Symmetric Elliptic Integrals," SIAM J. Math. Anls., vol. 25, no. 2,
2077 pp. 288-303, 1994.
2078 https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9310223
2079 https://doi.org/10.1137/S0036141092228477
2080  
2081 Examples
2082 --------
2083 Basic homogeneity property:
2084  
2085 >>> import numpy as np
2086 >>> from scipy.special import elliprj
2087  
2088 >>> x = 1.2 + 3.4j
2089 >>> y = 5.
2090 >>> z = 6.
2091 >>> p = 7.
2092 >>> scale = 0.3 - 0.4j
2093 >>> elliprj(scale*x, scale*y, scale*z, scale*p)
2094 (0.10834905565679157+0.19694950747103812j)
2095  
2096 >>> elliprj(x, y, z, p)*np.power(scale, -1.5)
2097 (0.10834905565679556+0.19694950747103854j)
2098  
2099 Reduction to simpler elliptic integral:
2100  
2101 >>> elliprj(x, y, z, z)
2102 (0.08288462362195129-0.028376809745123258j)
2103  
2104 >>> from scipy.special import elliprd
2105 >>> elliprd(x, y, z)
2106 (0.08288462362195136-0.028376809745123296j)
2107  
2108 All arguments coincide:
2109  
2110 >>> elliprj(x, x, x, x)
2111 (-0.03986825876151896-0.14051741840449586j)
2112  
2113 >>> np.power(x, -1.5)
2114 (-0.03986825876151894-0.14051741840449583j)
2115  
2116 """)

2119 r"""
2120 entr(x, out=None)
2121  
2122 Elementwise function for computing entropy.
2123  
2124 .. math:: \text{entr}(x) = \begin{cases} - x \log(x) & x > 0 \\ 0 & x = 0
2125 \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
2126  
2127 Parameters
2128 ----------
2129 x : ndarray
2130 Input array.
2131 out : ndarray, optional
2132 Optional output array for the function values
2133  
2134 Returns
2135 -------
2136 res : scalar or ndarray
2137 The value of the elementwise entropy function at the given points `x`.
2138  
2139 See Also
2140 --------
2141 kl_div, rel_entr, scipy.stats.entropy
2142  
2143 Notes
2144 -----
2145 .. versionadded:: 0.15.0
2146  
2147 This function is concave.
2148  
2149 The origin of this function is in convex programming; see [1]_.
2150 Given a probability distribution :math:`p_1, \ldots, p_n`,
2151 the definition of entropy in the context of *information theory* is
2152  
2153 .. math::
2154  
2155 \sum_{i = 1}^n \mathrm{entr}(p_i).
2156  
2157 To compute the latter quantity, use `scipy.stats.entropy`.
2158  
2159 References
2160 ----------
2161 .. [1] Boyd, Stephen and Lieven Vandenberghe. *Convex optimization*.
2162 Cambridge University Press, 2004.
2163 :doi:`https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804441`

2170 erfinv(y, out=None)
2171  
2172 Inverse of the error function.
2173  
2174 Computes the inverse of the error function.
2175  
2176 In the complex domain, there is no unique complex number w satisfying
2177 erf(w)=z. This indicates a true inverse function would be multivalued.
2178 When the domain restricts to the real, -1 < x < 1, there is a unique real
2179 number satisfying erf(erfinv(x)) = x.
2180  
2181 Parameters
2182 ----------
2183 y : ndarray
2184 Argument at which to evaluate. Domain: [-1, 1]
2185 out : ndarray, optional
2186 Optional output array for the function values
2187  
2188 Returns
2189 -------
2190 erfinv : scalar or ndarray
2191 The inverse of erf of y, element-wise
2192  
2193 See Also
2194 --------
2195 erf : Error function of a complex argument
2196 erfc : Complementary error function, ``1 - erf(x)``
2197 erfcinv : Inverse of the complementary error function
2198  
2199 Notes
2200 -----
2201 This function wraps the ``erf_inv`` routine from the
2202 Boost Math C++ library [1]_.
2203  
2204 References
2205 ----------
2206 .. [1] The Boost Developers. "Boost C++ Libraries". https://www.boost.org/.
2207  
2208 Examples
2209 --------
2210 >>> import numpy as np
2211 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
2212 >>> from scipy.special import erfinv, erf
2213  
2214 >>> erfinv(0.5)
2215 0.4769362762044699
2216  
2217 >>> y = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, num=9)
2218 >>> x = erfinv(y)
2219 >>> x
2220 array([ -inf, -0.81341985, -0.47693628, -0.22531206, 0. ,
2221 0.22531206, 0.47693628, 0.81341985, inf])
2222  
2223 Verify that ``erf(erfinv(y))`` is ``y``.
2224  
2225 >>> erf(x)
2226 array([-1. , -0.75, -0.5 , -0.25, 0. , 0.25, 0.5 , 0.75, 1. ])
2227  
2228 Plot the function:
2229  
2230 >>> y = np.linspace(-1, 1, 200)
2231 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
2232 >>> ax.plot(y, erfinv(y))
2233 >>> ax.grid(True)
2234 >>> ax.set_xlabel('y')
2235 >>> ax.set_title('erfinv(y)')
2236 >>> plt.show()
2237  
2238 """)

2242 """
2243 erfcinv(y, out=None)
2244  
2245 Inverse of the complementary error function.
2246  
2247 Computes the inverse of the complementary error function.
2248  
2249 In the complex domain, there is no unique complex number w satisfying
2250 erfc(w)=z. This indicates a true inverse function would be multivalued.
2251 When the domain restricts to the real, 0 < x < 2, there is a unique real
2252 number satisfying erfc(erfcinv(x)) = erfcinv(erfc(x)).
2253  
2254 It is related to inverse of the error function by erfcinv(1-x) = erfinv(x)
2255  
2256 Parameters
2257 ----------
2258 y : ndarray
2259 Argument at which to evaluate. Domain: [0, 2]
2260 out : ndarray, optional
2261 Optional output array for the function values
2262  
2263 Returns
2264 -------
2265 erfcinv : scalar or ndarray
2266 The inverse of erfc of y, element-wise
2267  
2268 See Also
2269 --------
2270 erf : Error function of a complex argument
2271 erfc : Complementary error function, ``1 - erf(x)``
2272 erfinv : Inverse of the error function
2273  
2274 Examples
2275 --------
2276 >>> import numpy as np
2277 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
2278 >>> from scipy.special import erfcinv
2279  
2280 >>> erfcinv(0.5)
2281 0.4769362762044699
2282  
2283 >>> y = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0, num=11)
2284 >>> erfcinv(y)
2285 array([ inf, 0.9061938 , 0.59511608, 0.37080716, 0.17914345,
2286 -0. , -0.17914345, -0.37080716, -0.59511608, -0.9061938 ,
2287 -inf])
2288  
2289 Plot the function:
2290  
2291 >>> y = np.linspace(0, 2, 200)
2292 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
2293 >>> ax.plot(y, erfcinv(y))
2294 >>> ax.grid(True)
2295 >>> ax.set_xlabel('y')
2296 >>> ax.set_title('erfcinv(y)')
2297 >>> plt.show()
2298  
2299 """)

2302 r"""
2303 eval_jacobi(n, alpha, beta, x, out=None)
2304  
2305 Evaluate Jacobi polynomial at a point.
2306  
2307 The Jacobi polynomials can be defined via the Gauss hypergeometric
2308 function :math:`{}_2F_1` as
2309  
2310 .. math::
2311  
2312 P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x) = \frac{(\alpha + 1)_n}{\Gamma(n + 1)}
2313 {}_2F_1(-n, 1 + \alpha + \beta + n; \alpha + 1; (1 - z)/2)
2314  
2315 where :math:`(\cdot)_n` is the Pochhammer symbol; see `poch`. When
2316 :math:`n` is an integer the result is a polynomial of degree
2317 :math:`n`. See 22.5.42 in [AS]_ for details.
2318  
2319 Parameters
2320 ----------
2321 n : array_like
2322 Degree of the polynomial. If not an integer the result is
2323 determined via the relation to the Gauss hypergeometric
2324 function.
2325 alpha : array_like
2326 Parameter
2327 beta : array_like
2328 Parameter
2329 x : array_like
2330 Points at which to evaluate the polynomial
2331 out : ndarray, optional
2332 Optional output array for the function values
2333  
2334 Returns
2335 -------
2336 P : scalar or ndarray
2337 Values of the Jacobi polynomial
2338  
2339 See Also
2340 --------
2341 roots_jacobi : roots and quadrature weights of Jacobi polynomials
2342 jacobi : Jacobi polynomial object
2343 hyp2f1 : Gauss hypergeometric function

2347 .. [AS] Milton Abramowitz and Irene A. Stegun, eds.
2348 Handbook of Mathematical Functions with Formulas,
2349 Graphs, and Mathematical Tables. New York: Dover, 1972.

2367 polynomial. See 22.5.2 in [AS]_ for details.

2773 The Legendre polynomials can be defined via the Gauss
2774 hypergeometric function :math:`{}_2F_1` as

2781 :math:`n`. See 22.5.49 in [AS]_ for details.

2792 Optional output array for the function values

2811 Graphs, and Mathematical Tables. New York: Dover, 1972.

2813 Examples
2814 --------
2815 >>> import numpy as np
2816 >>> from scipy.special import eval_legendre
2817  
2818 Evaluate the zero-order Legendre polynomial at x = 0
2819  
2820 >>> eval_legendre(0, 0)
2821 1.0
2822  
2823 Evaluate the first-order Legendre polynomial between -1 and 1
2824  
2825 >>> X = np.linspace(-1, 1, 5) # Domain of Legendre polynomials
2826 >>> eval_legendre(1, X)
2827 array([-1. , -0.5, 0. , 0.5, 1. ])
2828  
2829 Evaluate Legendre polynomials of order 0 through 4 at x = 0
2830  
2831 >>> N = range(0, 5)
2832 >>> eval_legendre(N, 0)
2833 array([ 1. , 0. , -0.5 , 0. , 0.375])
2834  
2835 Plot Legendre polynomials of order 0 through 4
2836  
2837 >>> X = np.linspace(-1, 1)
2838  
2839 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
2840 >>> for n in range(0, 5):
2841 ... y = eval_legendre(n, X)
2842 ... plt.plot(X, y, label=r'$P_{}(x)$'.format(n))
2843  
2844 >>> plt.title("Legendre Polynomials")
2845 >>> plt.xlabel("x")
2846 >>> plt.ylabel(r'$P_n(x)$')
2847 >>> plt.legend(loc='lower right')
2848 >>> plt.show()
2849

2904 The generalized Laguerre polynomials can be defined via the

2908

2910 {}_1F_1(-n, \alpha + 1, x).

2913 :math:`n`. See 22.5.54 in [AS]_ for details. The Laguerre
2914 polynomials are the special case where :math:`\alpha = 0`.

2926 polynomial

3091 r"""
3092 expn(n, x, out=None)
3093  
3094 Generalized exponential integral En.
3095  
3096 For integer :math:`n \geq 0` and real :math:`x \geq 0` the
3097 generalized exponential integral is defined as [dlmf]_
3098  
3099 .. math::
3100  
3101 E_n(x) = x^{n - 1} \int_x^\infty \frac{e^{-t}}{t^n} dt.
3102  
3103 Parameters
3104 ----------
3105 n : array_like
3106 Non-negative integers
3107 x : array_like
3108 Real argument
3109 out : ndarray, optional
3110 Optional output array for the function results
3111  
3112 Returns
3113 -------
3114 scalar or ndarray
3115 Values of the generalized exponential integral
3116  
3117 See Also
3118 --------
3119 exp1 : special case of :math:`E_n` for :math:`n = 1`
3120 expi : related to :math:`E_n` when :math:`n = 1`
3121  
3122 References
3123 ----------
3124 .. [dlmf] Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, 8.19.2
3125 https://dlmf.nist.gov/8.19#E2
3126  
3127 Examples
3128 --------
3129 >>> import numpy as np
3130 >>> import scipy.special as sc
3131  
3132 Its domain is nonnegative n and x.
3133  
3134 >>> sc.expn(-1, 1.0), sc.expn(1, -1.0)
3135 (nan, nan)
3136  
3137 It has a pole at ``x = 0`` for ``n = 1, 2``; for larger ``n`` it
3138 is equal to ``1 / (n - 1)``.
3139  
3140 >>> sc.expn([0, 1, 2, 3, 4], 0)
3141 array([ inf, inf, 1. , 0.5 , 0.33333333])
3142  
3143 For n equal to 0 it reduces to ``exp(-x) / x``.
3144  
3145 >>> x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
3146 >>> sc.expn(0, x)
3147 array([0.36787944, 0.06766764, 0.01659569, 0.00457891])
3148 >>> np.exp(-x) / x
3149 array([0.36787944, 0.06766764, 0.01659569, 0.00457891])
3150  
3151 For n equal to 1 it reduces to `exp1`.
3152  
3153 >>> sc.expn(1, x)
3154 array([0.21938393, 0.04890051, 0.01304838, 0.00377935])
3155 >>> sc.exp1(x)
3156 array([0.21938393, 0.04890051, 0.01304838, 0.00377935])
3157  
3158 """)

3160 add_newdoc("fdtr",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
3161 r"""
3162 fdtr(dfn, dfd, x, out=None)
3163  
3164 F cumulative distribution function.
3165  
3166 Returns the value of the cumulative distribution function of the
3167 F-distribution, also known as Snedecor's F-distribution or the
3168 Fisher-Snedecor distribution.
3169  
3170 The F-distribution with parameters :math:`d_n` and :math:`d_d` is the
3171 distribution of the random variable,
3172  
3173 .. math::
3174 X = \frac{U_n/d_n}{U_d/d_d},
3175  
3176 where :math:`U_n` and :math:`U_d` are random variables distributed
3177 :math:`\chi^2`, with :math:`d_n` and :math:`d_d` degrees of freedom,
3178 respectively.
3179  
3180 Parameters
3181 ----------
3182 dfn : array_like
3183 First parameter (positive float).
3184 dfd : array_like
3185 Second parameter (positive float).
3186 x : array_like
3187 Argument (nonnegative float).
3188 out : ndarray, optional
3189 Optional output array for the function values
3190  
3191 Returns
3192 -------
3193 y : scalar or ndarray
3194 The CDF of the F-distribution with parameters `dfn` and `dfd` at `x`.
3195  
3196 See Also
3197 --------
3198 fdtrc : F distribution survival function
3199 fdtri : F distribution inverse cumulative distribution
3200 scipy.stats.f : F distribution
3201  
3202 Notes
3203 -----
3204 The regularized incomplete beta function is used, according to the
3205 formula,
3206  
3207 .. math::
3208 F(d_n, d_d; x) = I_{xd_n/(d_d + xd_n)}(d_n/2, d_d/2).
3209  
3210 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `fdtr`. The F distribution is also
3211 available as `scipy.stats.f`. Calling `fdtr` directly can improve
3212 performance compared to the ``cdf`` method of `scipy.stats.f` (see last
3213 example below).
3214  
3215 References
3216 ----------
3217 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
3218 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
3219  
3220 Examples
3221 --------
3222 Calculate the function for ``dfn=1`` and ``dfd=2`` at ``x=1``.
3223  
3224 >>> import numpy as np
3225 >>> from scipy.special import fdtr
3226 >>> fdtr(1, 2, 1)
3227 0.5773502691896258
3228  
3229 Calculate the function at several points by providing a NumPy array for
3230 `x`.
3231  
3232 >>> x = np.array([0.5, 2., 3.])
3233 >>> fdtr(1, 2, x)
3234 array([0.4472136 , 0.70710678, 0.77459667])
3235  
3236 Plot the function for several parameter sets.
3237  
3238 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
3239 >>> dfn_parameters = [1, 5, 10, 50]
3240 >>> dfd_parameters = [1, 1, 2, 3]
3241 >>> linestyles = ['solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dashdot']
3242 >>> parameters_list = list(zip(dfn_parameters, dfd_parameters,
3243 ... linestyles))
3244 >>> x = np.linspace(0, 30, 1000)
3245 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
3246 >>> for parameter_set in parameters_list:
3247 ... dfn, dfd, style = parameter_set
3248 ... fdtr_vals = fdtr(dfn, dfd, x)
3249 ... ax.plot(x, fdtr_vals, label=rf"$d_n={dfn},\, d_d={dfd}$",
3250 ... ls=style)
3251 >>> ax.legend()
3252 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
3253 >>> ax.set_title("F distribution cumulative distribution function")
3254 >>> plt.show()
3255  
3256 The F distribution is also available as `scipy.stats.f`. Using `fdtr`
3257 directly can be much faster than calling the ``cdf`` method of
3258 `scipy.stats.f`, especially for small arrays or individual values.
3259 To get the same results one must use the following parametrization:
3260 ``stats.f(dfn, dfd).cdf(x)=fdtr(dfn, dfd, x)``.
3261  
3262 >>> from scipy.stats import f
3263 >>> dfn, dfd = 1, 2
3264 >>> x = 1
3265 >>> fdtr_res = fdtr(dfn, dfd, x) # this will often be faster than below
3266 >>> f_dist_res = f(dfn, dfd).cdf(x)
3267 >>> fdtr_res == f_dist_res # test that results are equal
3268 True
3269 """)
3270  
3271 add_newdoc("fdtrc",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
3272 r"""
3273 fdtrc(dfn, dfd, x, out=None)
3274  
3275 F survival function.
3276  
3277 Returns the complemented F-distribution function (the integral of the
3278 density from `x` to infinity).
3279  
3280 Parameters
3281 ----------
3282 dfn : array_like
3283 First parameter (positive float).
3284 dfd : array_like
3285 Second parameter (positive float).
3286 x : array_like
3287 Argument (nonnegative float).
3288 out : ndarray, optional
3289 Optional output array for the function values
3290  
3291 Returns
3292 -------
3293 y : scalar or ndarray
3294 The complemented F-distribution function with parameters `dfn` and
3295 `dfd` at `x`.
3296  
3297 See Also
3298 --------
3299 fdtr : F distribution cumulative distribution function
3300 fdtri : F distribution inverse cumulative distribution function
3301 scipy.stats.f : F distribution
3302  
3303 Notes
3304 -----
3305 The regularized incomplete beta function is used, according to the
3306 formula,
3307  
3308 .. math::
3309 F(d_n, d_d; x) = I_{d_d/(d_d + xd_n)}(d_d/2, d_n/2).
3310  
3311 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `fdtrc`. The F distribution is also
3312 available as `scipy.stats.f`. Calling `fdtrc` directly can improve
3313 performance compared to the ``sf`` method of `scipy.stats.f` (see last
3314 example below).
3315  
3316 References
3317 ----------
3318 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
3319 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
3320  
3321 Examples
3322 --------
3323 Calculate the function for ``dfn=1`` and ``dfd=2`` at ``x=1``.
3324  
3325 >>> import numpy as np
3326 >>> from scipy.special import fdtrc
3327 >>> fdtrc(1, 2, 1)
3328 0.42264973081037427
3329  
3330 Calculate the function at several points by providing a NumPy array for
3331 `x`.
3332  
3333 >>> x = np.array([0.5, 2., 3.])
3334 >>> fdtrc(1, 2, x)
3335 array([0.5527864 , 0.29289322, 0.22540333])
3336  
3337 Plot the function for several parameter sets.
3338  
3339 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
3340 >>> dfn_parameters = [1, 5, 10, 50]
3341 >>> dfd_parameters = [1, 1, 2, 3]
3342 >>> linestyles = ['solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dashdot']
3343 >>> parameters_list = list(zip(dfn_parameters, dfd_parameters,
3344 ... linestyles))
3345 >>> x = np.linspace(0, 30, 1000)
3346 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
3347 >>> for parameter_set in parameters_list:
3348 ... dfn, dfd, style = parameter_set
3349 ... fdtrc_vals = fdtrc(dfn, dfd, x)
3350 ... ax.plot(x, fdtrc_vals, label=rf"$d_n={dfn},\, d_d={dfd}$",
3351 ... ls=style)
3352 >>> ax.legend()
3353 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
3354 >>> ax.set_title("F distribution survival function")
3355 >>> plt.show()
3356  
3357 The F distribution is also available as `scipy.stats.f`. Using `fdtrc`
3358 directly can be much faster than calling the ``sf`` method of
3359 `scipy.stats.f`, especially for small arrays or individual values.
3360 To get the same results one must use the following parametrization:
3361 ``stats.f(dfn, dfd).sf(x)=fdtrc(dfn, dfd, x)``.
3362  
3363 >>> from scipy.stats import f
3364 >>> dfn, dfd = 1, 2
3365 >>> x = 1
3366 >>> fdtrc_res = fdtrc(dfn, dfd, x) # this will often be faster than below
3367 >>> f_dist_res = f(dfn, dfd).sf(x)
3368 >>> f_dist_res == fdtrc_res # test that results are equal
3369 True
3370 """)

3372 add_newdoc("fdtri",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
3373 r"""
3374 fdtri(dfn, dfd, p, out=None)
3375  
3376 The `p`-th quantile of the F-distribution.
3377  
3378 This function is the inverse of the F-distribution CDF, `fdtr`, returning
3379 the `x` such that `fdtr(dfn, dfd, x) = p`.
3380  
3381 Parameters
3382 ----------
3383 dfn : array_like
3384 First parameter (positive float).
3385 dfd : array_like
3386 Second parameter (positive float).
3387 p : array_like
3388 Cumulative probability, in [0, 1].
3389 out : ndarray, optional
3390 Optional output array for the function values
3391  
3392 Returns
3393 -------
3394 x : scalar or ndarray
3395 The quantile corresponding to `p`.
3396  
3397 See Also
3398 --------
3399 fdtr : F distribution cumulative distribution function
3400 fdtrc : F distribution survival function
3401 scipy.stats.f : F distribution
3402  
3403 Notes
3404 -----
3405 The computation is carried out using the relation to the inverse
3406 regularized beta function, :math:`I^{-1}_x(a, b)`. Let
3407 :math:`z = I^{-1}_p(d_d/2, d_n/2).` Then,
3408  
3409 .. math::
3410 x = \frac{d_d (1 - z)}{d_n z}.
3411  
3412 If `p` is such that :math:`x < 0.5`, the following relation is used
3413 instead for improved stability: let
3414 :math:`z' = I^{-1}_{1 - p}(d_n/2, d_d/2).` Then,
3415  
3416 .. math::
3417 x = \frac{d_d z'}{d_n (1 - z')}.
3418  
3419 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `fdtri`.
3420  
3421 The F distribution is also available as `scipy.stats.f`. Calling
3422 `fdtri` directly can improve performance compared to the ``ppf``
3423 method of `scipy.stats.f` (see last example below).
3424  
3425 References
3426 ----------
3427 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
3428 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
3429  
3430 Examples
3431 --------
3432 `fdtri` represents the inverse of the F distribution CDF which is
3433 available as `fdtr`. Here, we calculate the CDF for ``df1=1``, ``df2=2``
3434 at ``x=3``. `fdtri` then returns ``3`` given the same values for `df1`,
3435 `df2` and the computed CDF value.
3436  
3437 >>> import numpy as np
3438 >>> from scipy.special import fdtri, fdtr
3439 >>> df1, df2 = 1, 2
3440 >>> x = 3
3441 >>> cdf_value = fdtr(df1, df2, x)
3442 >>> fdtri(df1, df2, cdf_value)
3443 3.000000000000006
3444  
3445 Calculate the function at several points by providing a NumPy array for
3446 `x`.
3447  
3448 >>> x = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.7])
3449 >>> fdtri(1, 2, x)
3450 array([0.02020202, 0.38095238, 1.92156863])
3451  
3452 Plot the function for several parameter sets.
3453  
3454 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
3455 >>> dfn_parameters = [50, 10, 1, 50]
3456 >>> dfd_parameters = [0.5, 1, 1, 5]
3457 >>> linestyles = ['solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dashdot']
3458 >>> parameters_list = list(zip(dfn_parameters, dfd_parameters,
3459 ... linestyles))
3460 >>> x = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)
3461 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
3462 >>> for parameter_set in parameters_list:
3463 ... dfn, dfd, style = parameter_set
3464 ... fdtri_vals = fdtri(dfn, dfd, x)
3465 ... ax.plot(x, fdtri_vals, label=rf"$d_n={dfn},\, d_d={dfd}$",
3466 ... ls=style)
3467 >>> ax.legend()
3468 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
3469 >>> title = "F distribution inverse cumulative distribution function"
3470 >>> ax.set_title(title)
3471 >>> ax.set_ylim(0, 30)
3472 >>> plt.show()
3473  
3474 The F distribution is also available as `scipy.stats.f`. Using `fdtri`
3475 directly can be much faster than calling the ``ppf`` method of
3476 `scipy.stats.f`, especially for small arrays or individual values.
3477 To get the same results one must use the following parametrization:
3478 ``stats.f(dfn, dfd).ppf(x)=fdtri(dfn, dfd, x)``.
3479  
3480 >>> from scipy.stats import f
3481 >>> dfn, dfd = 1, 2
3482 >>> x = 0.7
3483 >>> fdtri_res = fdtri(dfn, dfd, x) # this will often be faster than below
3484 >>> f_dist_res = f(dfn, dfd).ppf(x)
3485 >>> f_dist_res == fdtri_res # test that results are equal
3486 True
3487 """)
3488

3575 add_newdoc("gdtr",

3576 r"""
3577 gdtr(a, b, x, out=None)
3578  
3579 Gamma distribution cumulative distribution function.
3580  
3581 Returns the integral from zero to `x` of the gamma probability density
3582 function,
3583  
3584 .. math::
3585  
3586 F = \int_0^x \frac{a^b}{\Gamma(b)} t^{b-1} e^{-at}\,dt,
3587  
3588 where :math:`\Gamma` is the gamma function.
3589  
3590 Parameters
3591 ----------
3592 a : array_like
3593 The rate parameter of the gamma distribution, sometimes denoted
3594 :math:`\beta` (float). It is also the reciprocal of the scale
3595 parameter :math:`\theta`.
3596 b : array_like
3597 The shape parameter of the gamma distribution, sometimes denoted
3598 :math:`\alpha` (float).
3599 x : array_like
3600 The quantile (upper limit of integration; float).
3601 out : ndarray, optional
3602 Optional output array for the function values
3603  
3604 Returns
3605 -------
3606 F : scalar or ndarray
3607 The CDF of the gamma distribution with parameters `a` and `b`
3608 evaluated at `x`.
3609  
3610 See Also
3611 --------
3612 gdtrc : 1 - CDF of the gamma distribution.
3613 scipy.stats.gamma: Gamma distribution
3614  
3615 Notes
3616 -----
3617 The evaluation is carried out using the relation to the incomplete gamma
3618 integral (regularized gamma function).
3619  
3620 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `gdtr`. Calling `gdtr` directly can
3621 improve performance compared to the ``cdf`` method of `scipy.stats.gamma`
3622 (see last example below).
3623  
3624 References
3625 ----------
3626 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
3627 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
3628  
3629 Examples
3630 --------
3631 Compute the function for ``a=1``, ``b=2`` at ``x=5``.
3632  
3633 >>> import numpy as np
3634 >>> from scipy.special import gdtr
3635 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
3636 >>> gdtr(1., 2., 5.)
3637 0.9595723180054873
3638  
3639 Compute the function for ``a=1`` and ``b=2`` at several points by
3640 providing a NumPy array for `x`.
3641  
3642 >>> xvalues = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4])
3643 >>> gdtr(1., 1., xvalues)
3644 array([0.63212056, 0.86466472, 0.95021293, 0.98168436])
3645  
3646 `gdtr` can evaluate different parameter sets by providing arrays with
3647 broadcasting compatible shapes for `a`, `b` and `x`. Here we compute the
3648 function for three different `a` at four positions `x` and ``b=3``,
3649 resulting in a 3x4 array.
3650  
3651 >>> a = np.array([[0.5], [1.5], [2.5]])
3652 >>> x = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4])
3653 >>> a.shape, x.shape
3654 ((3, 1), (4,))
3655  
3656 >>> gdtr(a, 3., x)
3657 array([[0.01438768, 0.0803014 , 0.19115317, 0.32332358],
3658 [0.19115317, 0.57680992, 0.82642193, 0.9380312 ],
3659 [0.45618688, 0.87534798, 0.97974328, 0.9972306 ]])
3660  
3661 Plot the function for four different parameter sets.
3662  
3663 >>> a_parameters = [0.3, 1, 2, 6]
3664 >>> b_parameters = [2, 10, 15, 20]
3665 >>> linestyles = ['solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dashdot']
3666 >>> parameters_list = list(zip(a_parameters, b_parameters, linestyles))
3667 >>> x = np.linspace(0, 30, 1000)
3668 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
3669 >>> for parameter_set in parameters_list:
3670 ... a, b, style = parameter_set
3671 ... gdtr_vals = gdtr(a, b, x)
3672 ... ax.plot(x, gdtr_vals, label=fr"$a= {a},\, b={b}$", ls=style)
3673 >>> ax.legend()
3674 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
3675 >>> ax.set_title("Gamma distribution cumulative distribution function")
3676 >>> plt.show()
3677  
3678 The gamma distribution is also available as `scipy.stats.gamma`. Using
3679 `gdtr` directly can be much faster than calling the ``cdf`` method of
3680 `scipy.stats.gamma`, especially for small arrays or individual values.
3681 To get the same results one must use the following parametrization:
3682 ``stats.gamma(b, scale=1/a).cdf(x)=gdtr(a, b, x)``.
3683  
3684 >>> from scipy.stats import gamma
3685 >>> a = 2.
3686 >>> b = 3
3687 >>> x = 1.
3688 >>> gdtr_result = gdtr(a, b, x) # this will often be faster than below
3689 >>> gamma_dist_result = gamma(b, scale=1/a).cdf(x)
3690 >>> gdtr_result == gamma_dist_result # test that results are equal
3691 True
3692 """)

3814 """
3815 gdtria(p, b, x, out=None)
3816  
3817 Inverse of `gdtr` vs a.
3818  
3819 Returns the inverse with respect to the parameter `a` of ``p =
3820 gdtr(a, b, x)``, the cumulative distribution function of the gamma
3821 distribution.
3822  
3823 Parameters
3824 ----------
3825 p : array_like
3826 Probability values.
3827 b : array_like
3828 `b` parameter values of `gdtr(a, b, x)`. `b` is the "shape" parameter
3829 of the gamma distribution.
3830 x : array_like
3831 Nonnegative real values, from the domain of the gamma distribution.
3832 out : ndarray, optional
3833 If a fourth argument is given, it must be a numpy.ndarray whose size
3834 matches the broadcast result of `a`, `b` and `x`. `out` is then the
3835 array returned by the function.
3836  
3837 Returns
3838 -------
3839 a : scalar or ndarray
3840 Values of the `a` parameter such that ``p = gdtr(a, b, x)`. ``1/a``
3841 is the "scale" parameter of the gamma distribution.
3842  
3843 See Also
3844 --------
3845 gdtr : CDF of the gamma distribution.
3846 gdtrib : Inverse with respect to `b` of `gdtr(a, b, x)`.
3847 gdtrix : Inverse with respect to `x` of `gdtr(a, b, x)`.
3848  
3849 Notes
3850 -----
3851 Wrapper for the CDFLIB [1]_ Fortran routine `cdfgam`.
3852  
3853 The cumulative distribution function `p` is computed using a routine by
3854 DiDinato and Morris [2]_. Computation of `a` involves a search for a value
3855 that produces the desired value of `p`. The search relies on the
3856 monotonicity of `p` with `a`.
3857  
3858 References
3859 ----------
3860 .. [1] Barry Brown, James Lovato, and Kathy Russell,
3861 CDFLIB: Library of Fortran Routines for Cumulative Distribution
3862 Functions, Inverses, and Other Parameters.
3863 .. [2] DiDinato, A. R. and Morris, A. H.,
3864 Computation of the incomplete gamma function ratios and their
3865 inverse. ACM Trans. Math. Softw. 12 (1986), 377-393.
3866  
3867 Examples
3868 --------
3869 First evaluate `gdtr`.
3870  
3871 >>> from scipy.special import gdtr, gdtria
3872 >>> p = gdtr(1.2, 3.4, 5.6)
3873 >>> print(p)
3874 0.94378087442
3875  
3876 Verify the inverse.
3877  
3878 >>> gdtria(p, 3.4, 5.6)
3879 1.2
3880 """)

3898 Probability values.

3904 array returned by the function.

3919 -----
3920  
3921 The cumulative distribution function `p` is computed using the Cephes [1]_
  • E501 Line too long (81 > 79 characters)
3922 routines `igam` and `igamc`. Computation of `b` involves a search for a value
3923 that produces the desired value of `p` using Chandrupatla's bracketing
3924 root finding algorithm [2]_.

3926 Note that there are some edge cases where `gdtrib` is extended by taking
3927 limits where they are uniquely defined. In particular
3928 ``x == 0`` with ``p > 0`` and ``p == 0`` with ``x > 0``.
3929 For these edge cases, a numerical result will be returned for
3930 ``gdtrib(a, p, x)`` even though ``gdtr(a, gdtrib(a, p, x), x)`` is
3931 undefined.

4216 huber(delta, r, out=None)
4217  
4218 Huber loss function.
4219  
4220 .. math:: \text{huber}(\delta, r) = \begin{cases} \infty & \delta < 0 \\
4221 \frac{1}{2}r^2 & 0 \le \delta, | r | \le \delta \\
4222 \delta ( |r| - \frac{1}{2}\delta ) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
4223  
4224 Parameters
4225 ----------
4226 delta : ndarray
4227 Input array, indicating the quadratic vs. linear loss changepoint.
4228 r : ndarray
4229 Input array, possibly representing residuals.
4230 out : ndarray, optional
4231 Optional output array for the function values
4232  
4233 Returns
4234 -------
4235 scalar or ndarray
4236 The computed Huber loss function values.
4237  
4238 See Also
4239 --------
4240 pseudo_huber : smooth approximation of this function
4241  
4242 Notes
4243 -----
4244 `huber` is useful as a loss function in robust statistics or machine
4245 learning to reduce the influence of outliers as compared to the common
4246 squared error loss, residuals with a magnitude higher than `delta` are
4247 not squared [1]_.
4248  
4249 Typically, `r` represents residuals, the difference
4250 between a model prediction and data. Then, for :math:`|r|\leq\delta`,
4251 `huber` resembles the squared error and for :math:`|r|>\delta` the
4252 absolute error. This way, the Huber loss often achieves
4253 a fast convergence in model fitting for small residuals like the squared
4254 error loss function and still reduces the influence of outliers
4255 (:math:`|r|>\delta`) like the absolute error loss. As :math:`\delta` is
4256 the cutoff between squared and absolute error regimes, it has
4257 to be tuned carefully for each problem. `huber` is also
4258 convex, making it suitable for gradient based optimization.
4259  
4260 .. versionadded:: 0.15.0
4261  
4262 References
4263 ----------
4264 .. [1] Peter Huber. "Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter",
4265 1964. Annals of Statistics. 53 (1): 73 - 101.
4266  
4267 Examples
4268 --------
4269 Import all necessary modules.
4270  
4271 >>> import numpy as np
4272 >>> from scipy.special import huber
4273 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
4274  
4275 Compute the function for ``delta=1`` at ``r=2``
4276  
4277 >>> huber(1., 2.)
4278 1.5
4279  
4280 Compute the function for different `delta` by providing a NumPy array or
4281 list for `delta`.
4282  
4283 >>> huber([1., 3., 5.], 4.)
4284 array([3.5, 7.5, 8. ])
4285  
4286 Compute the function at different points by providing a NumPy array or
4287 list for `r`.
4288  
4289 >>> huber(2., np.array([1., 1.5, 3.]))
4290 array([0.5 , 1.125, 4. ])
4291  
4292 The function can be calculated for different `delta` and `r` by
4293 providing arrays for both with compatible shapes for broadcasting.
4294  
4295 >>> r = np.array([1., 2.5, 8., 10.])
4296 >>> deltas = np.array([[1.], [5.], [9.]])
4297 >>> print(r.shape, deltas.shape)
4298 (4,) (3, 1)
4299  
4300 >>> huber(deltas, r)
4301 array([[ 0.5 , 2. , 7.5 , 9.5 ],
4302 [ 0.5 , 3.125, 27.5 , 37.5 ],
4303 [ 0.5 , 3.125, 32. , 49.5 ]])
4304  
4305 Plot the function for different `delta`.
4306  
4307 >>> x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 500)
4308 >>> deltas = [1, 2, 3]
4309 >>> linestyles = ["dashed", "dotted", "dashdot"]
4310 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
4311 >>> combined_plot_parameters = list(zip(deltas, linestyles))
4312 >>> for delta, style in combined_plot_parameters:
4313 ... ax.plot(x, huber(delta, x), label=fr"$\delta={delta}$", ls=style)
4314 >>> ax.legend(loc="upper center")
4315 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
4316 >>> ax.set_title(r"Huber loss function $h_{\delta}(x)$")
4317 >>> ax.set_xlim(-4, 4)
4318 >>> ax.set_ylim(0, 8)
4319 >>> plt.show()
4320 """)

4323 r"""
4324 hyp0f1(v, z, out=None)
4325  
4326 Confluent hypergeometric limit function 0F1.
4327  
4328 Parameters
4329 ----------
4330 v : array_like
4331 Real-valued parameter
4332 z : array_like
4333 Real- or complex-valued argument
4334 out : ndarray, optional
4335 Optional output array for the function results
4336  
4337 Returns
4338 -------
4339 scalar or ndarray
4340 The confluent hypergeometric limit function
4341  
4342 Notes
4343 -----
4344 This function is defined as:
4345  
4346 .. math:: _0F_1(v, z) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^k}{(v)_k k!}.
4347  
4348 It's also the limit as :math:`q \to \infty` of :math:`_1F_1(q; v; z/q)`,
4349 and satisfies the differential equation :math:`f''(z) + vf'(z) =
4350 f(z)`. See [1]_ for more information.
4351  
4352 References
4353 ----------
4354 .. [1] Wolfram MathWorld, "Confluent Hypergeometric Limit Function",
4355 http://mathworld.wolfram.com/ConfluentHypergeometricLimitFunction.html
4356  
4357 Examples
4358 --------
4359 >>> import numpy as np
4360 >>> import scipy.special as sc
4361  
4362 It is one when `z` is zero.
4363  
4364 >>> sc.hyp0f1(1, 0)
4365 1.0
4366  
4367 It is the limit of the confluent hypergeometric function as `q`
4368 goes to infinity.
4369  
4370 >>> q = np.array([1, 10, 100, 1000])
4371 >>> v = 1
4372 >>> z = 1
4373 >>> sc.hyp1f1(q, v, z / q)
4374 array([2.71828183, 2.31481985, 2.28303778, 2.27992985])
4375 >>> sc.hyp0f1(v, z)
4376 2.2795853023360673
4377  
4378 It is related to Bessel functions.
4379  
4380 >>> n = 1
4381 >>> x = np.linspace(0, 1, 5)
4382 >>> sc.jv(n, x)
4383 array([0. , 0.12402598, 0.24226846, 0.3492436 , 0.44005059])
4384 >>> (0.5 * x)**n / sc.factorial(n) * sc.hyp0f1(n + 1, -0.25 * x**2)
4385 array([0. , 0.12402598, 0.24226846, 0.3492436 , 0.44005059])
4386

4391 hyp1f1(a, b, x, out=None)

4398  
4399 {}_1F_1(a; b; x) = \sum_{k = 0}^\infty \frac{(a)_k}{(b)_k k!} x^k.
4400  
4401 See [dlmf]_ for more details. Here :math:`(\cdot)_k` is the
4402 Pochhammer symbol; see `poch`.
4403  
4404 Parameters

4424 Notes

4430 References
4431 ----------

4438 Examples
4439 --------

4460  
4461 It reduces to the exponential function when ``a = b``.

4472 hyperu(a, b, x, out=None)
4473  
4474 Confluent hypergeometric function U
4475  
4476 It is defined as the solution to the equation
4477  
4478 .. math::
4479  
4480 x \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} + (b - x) \frac{dw}{dx} - aw = 0
4481  
4482 which satisfies the property
4483  
4484 .. math::
4485  
4486 U(a, b, x) \sim x^{-a}
4487  
4488 as :math:`x \to \infty`. See [dlmf]_ for more details.
4489  
4490 Parameters
4491 ----------
4492 a, b : array_like
4493 Real-valued parameters
4494 x : array_like
4495 Real-valued argument
4496 out : ndarray, optional
4497 Optional output array for the function values
4498  
4499 Returns
4500 -------
4501 scalar or ndarray
4502 Values of `U`
4503  
4504 References
4505 ----------
4506 .. [dlmf] NIST Digital Library of Mathematics Functions
4507 https://dlmf.nist.gov/13.2#E6
4508  
4509 Examples
4510 --------
4511 >>> import numpy as np
4512 >>> import scipy.special as sc
4513  
4514 It has a branch cut along the negative `x` axis.
4515  
4516 >>> x = np.linspace(-0.1, -10, 5)
4517 >>> sc.hyperu(1, 1, x)
4518 array([nan, nan, nan, nan, nan])
4519  
4520 It approaches zero as `x` goes to infinity.
4521  
4522 >>> x = np.array([1, 10, 100])
4523 >>> sc.hyperu(1, 1, x)
4524 array([0.59634736, 0.09156333, 0.00990194])
4525  
4526 It satisfies Kummer's transformation.
4527  
4528 >>> a, b, x = 2, 1, 1
4529 >>> sc.hyperu(a, b, x)
4530 0.1926947246463881
4531 >>> x**(1 - b) * sc.hyperu(a - b + 1, 2 - b, x)
4532 0.1926947246463881

4542 r"""
4543 iv(v, z, out=None)
4544  
4545 Modified Bessel function of the first kind of real order.
4546  
4547 Parameters
4548 ----------
4549 v : array_like
4550 Order. If `z` is of real type and negative, `v` must be integer
4551 valued.
4552 z : array_like of float or complex
4553 Argument.
4554 out : ndarray, optional
4555 Optional output array for the function values
4556  
4557 Returns
4558 -------
4559 scalar or ndarray
4560 Values of the modified Bessel function.
4561  
4562 See Also
4563 --------
4564 ive : This function with leading exponential behavior stripped off.
4565 i0 : Faster version of this function for order 0.
4566 i1 : Faster version of this function for order 1.
4567  
4568 Notes
4569 -----
4570 For real `z` and :math:`v \in [-50, 50]`, the evaluation is carried out
4571 using Temme's method [1]_. For larger orders, uniform asymptotic
4572 expansions are applied.
4573  
4574 For complex `z` and positive `v`, the AMOS [2]_ `zbesi` routine is
4575 called. It uses a power series for small `z`, the asymptotic expansion
4576 for large `abs(z)`, the Miller algorithm normalized by the Wronskian
4577 and a Neumann series for intermediate magnitudes, and the uniform
4578 asymptotic expansions for :math:`I_v(z)` and :math:`J_v(z)` for large
4579 orders. Backward recurrence is used to generate sequences or reduce
4580 orders when necessary.
4581  
4582 The calculations above are done in the right half plane and continued
4583 into the left half plane by the formula,
4584  
4585 .. math:: I_v(z \exp(\pm\imath\pi)) = \exp(\pm\pi v) I_v(z)
4586  
4587 (valid when the real part of `z` is positive). For negative `v`, the
4588 formula
4589  
4590 .. math:: I_{-v}(z) = I_v(z) + \frac{2}{\pi} \sin(\pi v) K_v(z)
4591  
4592 is used, where :math:`K_v(z)` is the modified Bessel function of the
4593 second kind, evaluated using the AMOS routine `zbesk`.
4594  
4595 References
4596 ----------
4597 .. [1] Temme, Journal of Computational Physics, vol 21, 343 (1976)
4598 .. [2] Donald E. Amos, "AMOS, A Portable Package for Bessel Functions
4599 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",
4600 http://netlib.org/amos/
4601  
4602 Examples
4603 --------
4604 Evaluate the function of order 0 at one point.
4605  
4606 >>> from scipy.special import iv
4607 >>> iv(0, 1.)
4608 1.2660658777520084
4609  
4610 Evaluate the function at one point for different orders.
4611  
4612 >>> iv(0, 1.), iv(1, 1.), iv(1.5, 1.)
4613 (1.2660658777520084, 0.565159103992485, 0.2935253263474798)
4614  
4615 The evaluation for different orders can be carried out in one call by
4616 providing a list or NumPy array as argument for the `v` parameter:
4617  
4618 >>> iv([0, 1, 1.5], 1.)
4619 array([1.26606588, 0.5651591 , 0.29352533])
4620  
4621 Evaluate the function at several points for order 0 by providing an
4622 array for `z`.
4623  
4624 >>> import numpy as np
4625 >>> points = np.array([-2., 0., 3.])
4626 >>> iv(0, points)
4627 array([2.2795853 , 1. , 4.88079259])
4628  
4629 If `z` is an array, the order parameter `v` must be broadcastable to
4630 the correct shape if different orders shall be computed in one call.
4631 To calculate the orders 0 and 1 for an 1D array:
4632  
4633 >>> orders = np.array([[0], [1]])
4634 >>> orders.shape
4635 (2, 1)
4636  
4637 >>> iv(orders, points)
4638 array([[ 2.2795853 , 1. , 4.88079259],
4639 [-1.59063685, 0. , 3.95337022]])
4640  
4641 Plot the functions of order 0 to 3 from -5 to 5.
4642  
4643 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
4644 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
4645 >>> x = np.linspace(-5., 5., 1000)
4646 >>> for i in range(4):
4647 ... ax.plot(x, iv(i, x), label=f'$I_{i!r}$')
4648 >>> ax.legend()
4649 >>> plt.show()
4650  
4651 """)
