4654 r"""
4655 ive(v, z, out=None)
4656  
4657 Exponentially scaled modified Bessel function of the first kind.
4658  
4659 Defined as::
4660  
4661 ive(v, z) = iv(v, z) * exp(-abs(z.real))
4662  
4663 For imaginary numbers without a real part, returns the unscaled
4664 Bessel function of the first kind `iv`.
4665  
4666 Parameters
4667 ----------
4668 v : array_like of float
4669 Order.
4670 z : array_like of float or complex
4671 Argument.
4672 out : ndarray, optional
4673 Optional output array for the function values
4674  
4675 Returns
4676 -------
4677 scalar or ndarray
4678 Values of the exponentially scaled modified Bessel function.
4679  
4680 See Also
4681 --------
4682 iv: Modified Bessel function of the first kind
4683 i0e: Faster implementation of this function for order 0
4684 i1e: Faster implementation of this function for order 1
4685  
4686 Notes
4687 -----
4688 For positive `v`, the AMOS [1]_ `zbesi` routine is called. It uses a
4689 power series for small `z`, the asymptotic expansion for large
4690 `abs(z)`, the Miller algorithm normalized by the Wronskian and a
4691 Neumann series for intermediate magnitudes, and the uniform asymptotic
4692 expansions for :math:`I_v(z)` and :math:`J_v(z)` for large orders.
4693 Backward recurrence is used to generate sequences or reduce orders when
4694 necessary.
4695  
4696 The calculations above are done in the right half plane and continued
4697 into the left half plane by the formula,
4698  
4699 .. math:: I_v(z \exp(\pm\imath\pi)) = \exp(\pm\pi v) I_v(z)
4700  
4701 (valid when the real part of `z` is positive). For negative `v`, the
4702 formula
4703  
4704 .. math:: I_{-v}(z) = I_v(z) + \frac{2}{\pi} \sin(\pi v) K_v(z)
4705  
4706 is used, where :math:`K_v(z)` is the modified Bessel function of the
4707 second kind, evaluated using the AMOS routine `zbesk`.
4708  
4709 `ive` is useful for large arguments `z`: for these, `iv` easily overflows,
4710 while `ive` does not due to the exponential scaling.
4711  
4712 References
4713 ----------
4714 .. [1] Donald E. Amos, "AMOS, A Portable Package for Bessel Functions
4715 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",
4716 http://netlib.org/amos/
4717  
4718 Examples
4719 --------
4720 In the following example `iv` returns infinity whereas `ive` still returns
4721 a finite number.
4722  
4723 >>> from scipy.special import iv, ive
4724 >>> import numpy as np
4725 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
4726 >>> iv(3, 1000.), ive(3, 1000.)
4727 (inf, 0.01256056218254712)
4728  
4729 Evaluate the function at one point for different orders by
4730 providing a list or NumPy array as argument for the `v` parameter:
4731  
4732 >>> ive([0, 1, 1.5], 1.)
4733 array([0.46575961, 0.20791042, 0.10798193])
4734  
4735 Evaluate the function at several points for order 0 by providing an
4736 array for `z`.
4737  
4738 >>> points = np.array([-2., 0., 3.])
4739 >>> ive(0, points)
4740 array([0.30850832, 1. , 0.24300035])
4741  
4742 Evaluate the function at several points for different orders by
4743 providing arrays for both `v` for `z`. Both arrays have to be
4744 broadcastable to the correct shape. To calculate the orders 0, 1
4745 and 2 for a 1D array of points:
4746  
4747 >>> ive([[0], [1], [2]], points)
4748 array([[ 0.30850832, 1. , 0.24300035],
4749 [-0.21526929, 0. , 0.19682671],
4750 [ 0.09323903, 0. , 0.11178255]])
4751  
4752 Plot the functions of order 0 to 3 from -5 to 5.
4753  
4754 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
4755 >>> x = np.linspace(-5., 5., 1000)
4756 >>> for i in range(4):
4757 ... ax.plot(x, ive(i, x), label=fr'$I_{i!r}(z)\cdot e^{{-|z|}}$')
4758 >>> ax.legend()
4759 >>> ax.set_xlabel(r"$z$")
4760 >>> plt.show()
4761 """)

4797 r"""
4798 jv(v, z, out=None)
4799  
4800 Bessel function of the first kind of real order and complex argument.
4801  
4802 Parameters
4803 ----------
4804 v : array_like
4805 Order (float).
4806 z : array_like
4807 Argument (float or complex).
4808 out : ndarray, optional
4809 Optional output array for the function values
4810  
4811 Returns
4812 -------
4813 J : scalar or ndarray
4814 Value of the Bessel function, :math:`J_v(z)`.
4815  
4816 See Also
4817 --------
4818 jve : :math:`J_v` with leading exponential behavior stripped off.
4819 spherical_jn : spherical Bessel functions.
4820 j0 : faster version of this function for order 0.
4821 j1 : faster version of this function for order 1.
4822  
4823 Notes
4824 -----
4825 For positive `v` values, the computation is carried out using the AMOS
4826 [1]_ `zbesj` routine, which exploits the connection to the modified
4827 Bessel function :math:`I_v`,
4828  
4829 .. math::
4830 J_v(z) = \exp(v\pi\imath/2) I_v(-\imath z)\qquad (\Im z > 0)
4831  
4832 J_v(z) = \exp(-v\pi\imath/2) I_v(\imath z)\qquad (\Im z < 0)
4833  
4834 For negative `v` values the formula,
4835  
4836 .. math:: J_{-v}(z) = J_v(z) \cos(\pi v) - Y_v(z) \sin(\pi v)
4837  
4838 is used, where :math:`Y_v(z)` is the Bessel function of the second
4839 kind, computed using the AMOS routine `zbesy`. Note that the second
4840 term is exactly zero for integer `v`; to improve accuracy the second
4841 term is explicitly omitted for `v` values such that `v = floor(v)`.
4842

4848 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",

  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
4903 r"""
4904 jve(v, z, out=None)
4905  
4906 Exponentially scaled Bessel function of the first kind of order `v`.
4907  
4908 Defined as::
4909  
4910 jve(v, z) = jv(v, z) * exp(-abs(z.imag))
4911  
4912 Parameters
4913 ----------
4914 v : array_like
4915 Order (float).
4916 z : array_like
4917 Argument (float or complex).
4918 out : ndarray, optional
4919 Optional output array for the function values
4920  
4921 Returns
4922 -------
4923 J : scalar or ndarray
4924 Value of the exponentially scaled Bessel function.
4925  
4926 See Also
4927 --------
4928 jv: Unscaled Bessel function of the first kind
4929  
4930 Notes
4931 -----
4932 For positive `v` values, the computation is carried out using the AMOS
4933 [1]_ `zbesj` routine, which exploits the connection to the modified
4934 Bessel function :math:`I_v`,
4935  
4936 .. math::
4937 J_v(z) = \exp(v\pi\imath/2) I_v(-\imath z)\qquad (\Im z > 0)
4938  
4939 J_v(z) = \exp(-v\pi\imath/2) I_v(\imath z)\qquad (\Im z < 0)
4940  
4941 For negative `v` values the formula,
4942  
4943 .. math:: J_{-v}(z) = J_v(z) \cos(\pi v) - Y_v(z) \sin(\pi v)
4944  
4945 is used, where :math:`Y_v(z)` is the Bessel function of the second
4946 kind, computed using the AMOS routine `zbesy`. Note that the second
4947 term is exactly zero for integer `v`; to improve accuracy the second
4948 term is explicitly omitted for `v` values such that `v = floor(v)`.
4949  
4950 Exponentially scaled Bessel functions are useful for large arguments `z`:
4951 for these, the unscaled Bessel functions can easily under-or overflow.
4952  
4953 References
4954 ----------
4955 .. [1] Donald E. Amos, "AMOS, A Portable Package for Bessel Functions
4956 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",
4957 http://netlib.org/amos/
4958  
4959 Examples
4960 --------
4961 Compare the output of `jv` and `jve` for large complex arguments for `z`
4962 by computing their values for order ``v=1`` at ``z=1000j``. We see that
4963 `jv` overflows but `jve` returns a finite number:
4964  
4965 >>> import numpy as np
4966 >>> from scipy.special import jv, jve
4967 >>> v = 1
4968 >>> z = 1000j
4969 >>> jv(v, z), jve(v, z)
4970 ((inf+infj), (7.721967686709077e-19+0.012610930256928629j))
4971  
4972 For real arguments for `z`, `jve` returns the same as `jv`.
4973  
4974 >>> v, z = 1, 1000
4975 >>> jv(v, z), jve(v, z)
4976 (0.004728311907089523, 0.004728311907089523)
4977  
4978 The function can be evaluated for several orders at the same time by
4979 providing a list or NumPy array for `v`:
4980  
4981 >>> jve([1, 3, 5], 1j)
4982 array([1.27304208e-17+2.07910415e-01j, -4.99352086e-19-8.15530777e-03j,
4983 6.11480940e-21+9.98657141e-05j])
4984  
4985 In the same way, the function can be evaluated at several points in one
4986 call by providing a list or NumPy array for `z`:
4987  
4988 >>> jve(1, np.array([1j, 2j, 3j]))
4989 array([1.27308412e-17+0.20791042j, 1.31814423e-17+0.21526929j,
4990 1.20521602e-17+0.19682671j])
4991  
4992 It is also possible to evaluate several orders at several points
4993 at the same time by providing arrays for `v` and `z` with
4994 compatible shapes for broadcasting. Compute `jve` for two different orders
4995 `v` and three points `z` resulting in a 2x3 array.
4996  
4997 >>> v = np.array([[1], [3]])
4998 >>> z = np.array([1j, 2j, 3j])
4999 >>> v.shape, z.shape
5000 ((2, 1), (3,))
5001  
5002 >>> jve(v, z)
5003 array([[1.27304208e-17+0.20791042j, 1.31810070e-17+0.21526929j,
5004 1.20517622e-17+0.19682671j],
5005 [-4.99352086e-19-0.00815531j, -1.76289571e-18-0.02879122j,
5006 -2.92578784e-18-0.04778332j]])
5007 """)

5115 r"""
5116 kl_div(x, y, out=None)
5117  
5118 Elementwise function for computing Kullback-Leibler divergence.
5119  
5120 .. math::
5121  
5122 \mathrm{kl\_div}(x, y) =
5123 \begin{cases}
5124 x \log(x / y) - x + y & x > 0, y > 0 \\
5125 y & x = 0, y \ge 0 \\
5126 \infty & \text{otherwise}
5127 \end{cases}
5128  
5129 Parameters
5130 ----------
5131 x, y : array_like
5132 Real arguments
5133 out : ndarray, optional
5134 Optional output array for the function results
5135  
5136 Returns
5137 -------
5138 scalar or ndarray
5139 Values of the Kullback-Liebler divergence.
5140  
5141 See Also
5142 --------
5143 entr, rel_entr, scipy.stats.entropy
5144  
5145 Notes
5146 -----
5147 .. versionadded:: 0.15.0
5148  
5149 This function is non-negative and is jointly convex in `x` and `y`.
5150  
5151 The origin of this function is in convex programming; see [1]_ for
5152 details. This is why the function contains the extra :math:`-x
5153 + y` terms over what might be expected from the Kullback-Leibler
5154 divergence. For a version of the function without the extra terms,
5155 see `rel_entr`.
5156  
5157 References
5158 ----------
5159 .. [1] Boyd, Stephen and Lieven Vandenberghe. *Convex optimization*.
5160 Cambridge University Press, 2004.
5161 :doi:`https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804441`
5162  
5163 """)

5278 kolmogorov(y, out=None)
5279  
5280 Complementary cumulative distribution (Survival Function) function of
5281 Kolmogorov distribution.
5282  
5283 Returns the complementary cumulative distribution function of
5284 Kolmogorov's limiting distribution (``D_n*\sqrt(n)`` as n goes to infinity)
5285 of a two-sided test for equality between an empirical and a theoretical
5286 distribution. It is equal to the (limit as n->infinity of the)
5287 probability that ``sqrt(n) * max absolute deviation > y``.
5288  
5289 Parameters
5290 ----------
5291 y : float array_like
5292 Absolute deviation between the Empirical CDF (ECDF) and the target CDF,
5293 multiplied by sqrt(n).
5294 out : ndarray, optional
5295 Optional output array for the function results
5296  
5297 Returns
5298 -------
5299 scalar or ndarray
5300 The value(s) of kolmogorov(y)
5301  
5302 See Also
5303 --------
5304 kolmogi : The Inverse Survival Function for the distribution
  • E501 Line too long (83 > 79 characters)
5305 scipy.stats.kstwobign : Provides the functionality as a continuous distribution

5309 -----
5310 `kolmogorov` is used by `stats.kstest` in the application of the
5311 Kolmogorov-Smirnov Goodness of Fit test. For historical reasons this
5312 function is exposed in `scpy.special`, but the recommended way to achieve
5313 the most accurate CDF/SF/PDF/PPF/ISF computations is to use the
5314 `stats.kstwobign` distribution.
5315

5318 Show the probability of a gap at least as big as 0, 0.5 and 1.0.

5320 >>> import numpy as np
5321 >>> from scipy.special import kolmogorov
5322 >>> from scipy.stats import kstwobign
5323 >>> kolmogorov([0, 0.5, 1.0])
5324 array([ 1. , 0.96394524, 0.26999967])

  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
5388 r"""
5389 kv(v, z, out=None)
5390  
5391 Modified Bessel function of the second kind of real order `v`
5392  
5393 Returns the modified Bessel function of the second kind for real order
5394 `v` at complex `z`.
5395  
5396 These are also sometimes called functions of the third kind, Basset
5397 functions, or Macdonald functions. They are defined as those solutions
5398 of the modified Bessel equation for which,
5399  
5400 .. math::
5401 K_v(x) \sim \sqrt{\pi/(2x)} \exp(-x)
5402  
5403 as :math:`x \to \infty` [3]_.
5404  
5405 Parameters
5406 ----------
5407 v : array_like of float
5408 Order of Bessel functions
5409 z : array_like of complex
5410 Argument at which to evaluate the Bessel functions
5411 out : ndarray, optional
5412 Optional output array for the function results
5413  
5414 Returns
5415 -------
5416 scalar or ndarray
5417 The results. Note that input must be of complex type to get complex
5418 output, e.g. ``kv(3, -2+0j)`` instead of ``kv(3, -2)``.
5419  
5420 See Also
5421 --------
5422 kve : This function with leading exponential behavior stripped off.
5423 kvp : Derivative of this function
5424  
5425 Notes
5426 -----
5427 Wrapper for AMOS [1]_ routine `zbesk`. For a discussion of the
5428 algorithm used, see [2]_ and the references therein.
5429  
5430 References
5431 ----------
5432 .. [1] Donald E. Amos, "AMOS, A Portable Package for Bessel Functions
5433 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",
5434 http://netlib.org/amos/
5435 .. [2] Donald E. Amos, "Algorithm 644: A portable package for Bessel
5436 functions of a complex argument and nonnegative order", ACM
5437 TOMS Vol. 12 Issue 3, Sept. 1986, p. 265
5438 .. [3] NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions,
5439 Eq. 10.25.E3. https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.25.E3
5440  
5441 Examples
5442 --------
5443 Plot the function of several orders for real input:
5444  
5445 >>> import numpy as np
5446 >>> from scipy.special import kv
5447 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
5448 >>> x = np.linspace(0, 5, 1000)
5449 >>> for N in np.linspace(0, 6, 5):
5450 ... plt.plot(x, kv(N, x), label='$K_{{{}}}(x)$'.format(N))
5451 >>> plt.ylim(0, 10)
5452 >>> plt.legend()
5453 >>> plt.title(r'Modified Bessel function of the second kind $K_\nu(x)$')
5454 >>> plt.show()
5455  
5456 Calculate for a single value at multiple orders:
5457  
5458 >>> kv([4, 4.5, 5], 1+2j)
5459 array([ 0.1992+2.3892j, 2.3493+3.6j , 7.2827+3.8104j])
5460  
5461 """)

5464 r"""
5465 kve(v, z, out=None)
5466  
5467 Exponentially scaled modified Bessel function of the second kind.
5468  
5469 Returns the exponentially scaled, modified Bessel function of the
5470 second kind (sometimes called the third kind) for real order `v` at
5471 complex `z`::
5472  
5473 kve(v, z) = kv(v, z) * exp(z)
5474  
5475 Parameters
5476 ----------
5477 v : array_like of float
5478 Order of Bessel functions
5479 z : array_like of complex
5480 Argument at which to evaluate the Bessel functions
5481 out : ndarray, optional
5482 Optional output array for the function results
5483  
5484 Returns
5485 -------
5486 scalar or ndarray
5487 The exponentially scaled modified Bessel function of the second kind.
5488  
5489 See Also
5490 --------
5491 kv : This function without exponential scaling.
5492 k0e : Faster version of this function for order 0.
5493 k1e : Faster version of this function for order 1.
5494  
5495 Notes
5496 -----
5497 Wrapper for AMOS [1]_ routine `zbesk`. For a discussion of the
5498 algorithm used, see [2]_ and the references therein.
5499  
5500 References
5501 ----------
5502 .. [1] Donald E. Amos, "AMOS, A Portable Package for Bessel Functions
5503 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",
5504 http://netlib.org/amos/
5505 .. [2] Donald E. Amos, "Algorithm 644: A portable package for Bessel
5506 functions of a complex argument and nonnegative order", ACM
5507 TOMS Vol. 12 Issue 3, Sept. 1986, p. 265
5508  
5509 Examples
5510 --------
5511 In the following example `kv` returns 0 whereas `kve` still returns
5512 a useful finite number.
5513  
5514 >>> import numpy as np
5515 >>> from scipy.special import kv, kve
5516 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
5517 >>> kv(3, 1000.), kve(3, 1000.)
5518 (0.0, 0.03980696128440973)
5519  
5520 Evaluate the function at one point for different orders by
5521 providing a list or NumPy array as argument for the `v` parameter:
5522  
5523 >>> kve([0, 1, 1.5], 1.)
5524 array([1.14446308, 1.63615349, 2.50662827])
5525  
5526 Evaluate the function at several points for order 0 by providing an
5527 array for `z`.
5528  
5529 >>> points = np.array([1., 3., 10.])
5530 >>> kve(0, points)
5531 array([1.14446308, 0.6977616 , 0.39163193])
5532  
5533 Evaluate the function at several points for different orders by
5534 providing arrays for both `v` for `z`. Both arrays have to be
5535 broadcastable to the correct shape. To calculate the orders 0, 1
5536 and 2 for a 1D array of points:
5537  
5538 >>> kve([[0], [1], [2]], points)
5539 array([[1.14446308, 0.6977616 , 0.39163193],
5540 [1.63615349, 0.80656348, 0.41076657],
5541 [4.41677005, 1.23547058, 0.47378525]])
5542  
5543 Plot the functions of order 0 to 3 from 0 to 5.

5671 add_newdoc("lpmv",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
5672 r"""
5673 lpmv(m, v, x, out=None)
5674  
5675 Associated Legendre function of integer order and real degree.
5676  
5677 Defined as
5678  
5679 .. math::
5680  
5681 P_v^m = (-1)^m (1 - x^2)^{m/2} \frac{d^m}{dx^m} P_v(x)
5682  
5683 where
5684  
5685 .. math::
5686  
5687 P_v = \sum_{k = 0}^\infty \frac{(-v)_k (v + 1)_k}{(k!)^2}
5688 \left(\frac{1 - x}{2}\right)^k
5689  
5690 is the Legendre function of the first kind. Here :math:`(\cdot)_k`
5691 is the Pochhammer symbol; see `poch`.
5692  
5693 Parameters
5694 ----------
5695 m : array_like
5696 Order (int or float). If passed a float not equal to an
5697 integer the function returns NaN.
5698 v : array_like
5699 Degree (float).
5700 x : array_like
5701 Argument (float). Must have ``|x| <= 1``.
5702 out : ndarray, optional
5703 Optional output array for the function results
5704  
5705 Returns
5706 -------
5707 pmv : scalar or ndarray
5708 Value of the associated Legendre function.
5709  
5710 See Also
5711 --------
5712 lpmn : Compute the associated Legendre function for all orders
5713 ``0, ..., m`` and degrees ``0, ..., n``.
5714 clpmn : Compute the associated Legendre function at complex
5715 arguments.
5716  
5717 Notes
5718 -----
5719 Note that this implementation includes the Condon-Shortley phase.
5720  
5721 References
5722 ----------
5723 .. [1] Zhang, Jin, "Computation of Special Functions", John Wiley
5724 and Sons, Inc, 1996.
5725  
5726 """)

5728 add_newdoc("nbdtr",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
5729 r"""
5730 nbdtr(k, n, p, out=None)
5731  
5732 Negative binomial cumulative distribution function.
5733  
5734 Returns the sum of the terms 0 through `k` of the negative binomial
5735 distribution probability mass function,
5736  
5737 .. math::
5738  
5739 F = \sum_{j=0}^k {{n + j - 1}\choose{j}} p^n (1 - p)^j.
5740  
5741 In a sequence of Bernoulli trials with individual success probabilities
5742 `p`, this is the probability that `k` or fewer failures precede the nth
5743 success.
5744  
5745 Parameters
5746 ----------
5747 k : array_like
5748 The maximum number of allowed failures (nonnegative int).
5749 n : array_like
5750 The target number of successes (positive int).
5751 p : array_like
5752 Probability of success in a single event (float).
5753 out : ndarray, optional
5754 Optional output array for the function results
5755  
5756 Returns
5757 -------
5758 F : scalar or ndarray
5759 The probability of `k` or fewer failures before `n` successes in a
5760 sequence of events with individual success probability `p`.
5761  
5762 See Also
5763 --------
5764 nbdtrc : Negative binomial survival function
5765 nbdtrik : Negative binomial quantile function
5766 scipy.stats.nbinom : Negative binomial distribution
5767  
5768 Notes
5769 -----
5770 If floating point values are passed for `k` or `n`, they will be truncated
5771 to integers.
5772  
5773 The terms are not summed directly; instead the regularized incomplete beta
5774 function is employed, according to the formula,
5775  
5776 .. math::
5777 \mathrm{nbdtr}(k, n, p) = I_{p}(n, k + 1).
5778  
5779 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `nbdtr`.
5780  
5781 The negative binomial distribution is also available as
5782 `scipy.stats.nbinom`. Using `nbdtr` directly can improve performance
5783 compared to the ``cdf`` method of `scipy.stats.nbinom` (see last example).
5784  
5785 References
5786 ----------
5787 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
5788 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
5789  
5790 Examples
5791 --------
5792 Compute the function for ``k=10`` and ``n=5`` at ``p=0.5``.
5793  
5794 >>> import numpy as np
5795 >>> from scipy.special import nbdtr
5796 >>> nbdtr(10, 5, 0.5)
5797 0.940765380859375
5798  
5799 Compute the function for ``n=10`` and ``p=0.5`` at several points by
5800 providing a NumPy array or list for `k`.
5801  
5802 >>> nbdtr([5, 10, 15], 10, 0.5)
5803 array([0.15087891, 0.58809853, 0.88523853])
5804  
5805 Plot the function for four different parameter sets.
5806  
5807 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
5808 >>> k = np.arange(130)
5809 >>> n_parameters = [20, 20, 20, 80]
5810 >>> p_parameters = [0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.5]
5811 >>> linestyles = ['solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dashdot']
5812 >>> parameters_list = list(zip(p_parameters, n_parameters,
5813 ... linestyles))
5814 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
5815 >>> for parameter_set in parameters_list:
5816 ... p, n, style = parameter_set
5817 ... nbdtr_vals = nbdtr(k, n, p)
5818 ... ax.plot(k, nbdtr_vals, label=rf"$n={n},\, p={p}$",
5819 ... ls=style)
5820 >>> ax.legend()
5821 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$k$")
5822 >>> ax.set_title("Negative binomial cumulative distribution function")
5823 >>> plt.show()
5824  
5825 The negative binomial distribution is also available as
5826 `scipy.stats.nbinom`. Using `nbdtr` directly can be much faster than
5827 calling the ``cdf`` method of `scipy.stats.nbinom`, especially for small
5828 arrays or individual values. To get the same results one must use the
5829 following parametrization: ``nbinom(n, p).cdf(k)=nbdtr(k, n, p)``.
5830  
5831 >>> from scipy.stats import nbinom
5832 >>> k, n, p = 5, 3, 0.5
5833 >>> nbdtr_res = nbdtr(k, n, p) # this will often be faster than below
5834 >>> stats_res = nbinom(n, p).cdf(k)
5835 >>> stats_res, nbdtr_res # test that results are equal
5836 (0.85546875, 0.85546875)
5837  
5838 `nbdtr` can evaluate different parameter sets by providing arrays with
5839 shapes compatible for broadcasting for `k`, `n` and `p`. Here we compute
5840 the function for three different `k` at four locations `p`, resulting in
5841 a 3x4 array.
5842  
5843 >>> k = np.array([[5], [10], [15]])
5844 >>> p = np.array([0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9])
5845 >>> k.shape, p.shape
5846 ((3, 1), (4,))
5847  
5848 >>> nbdtr(k, 5, p)
5849 array([[0.15026833, 0.62304687, 0.95265101, 0.9998531 ],
5850 [0.48450894, 0.94076538, 0.99932777, 0.99999999],
5851 [0.76249222, 0.99409103, 0.99999445, 1. ]])
5852 """)
5853  
5854 add_newdoc("nbdtrc",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
5855 r"""
5856 nbdtrc(k, n, p, out=None)
5857  
5858 Negative binomial survival function.
5859  
5860 Returns the sum of the terms `k + 1` to infinity of the negative binomial
5861 distribution probability mass function,
5862  
5863 .. math::
5864  
5865 F = \sum_{j=k + 1}^\infty {{n + j - 1}\choose{j}} p^n (1 - p)^j.
5866  
5867 In a sequence of Bernoulli trials with individual success probabilities
5868 `p`, this is the probability that more than `k` failures precede the nth
5869 success.
5870  
5871 Parameters
5872 ----------
5873 k : array_like
5874 The maximum number of allowed failures (nonnegative int).
5875 n : array_like
5876 The target number of successes (positive int).
5877 p : array_like
5878 Probability of success in a single event (float).
5879 out : ndarray, optional
5880 Optional output array for the function results
5881  
5882 Returns
5883 -------
5884 F : scalar or ndarray
5885 The probability of `k + 1` or more failures before `n` successes in a
5886 sequence of events with individual success probability `p`.
5887  
5888 See Also
5889 --------
5890 nbdtr : Negative binomial cumulative distribution function
5891 nbdtrik : Negative binomial percentile function
5892 scipy.stats.nbinom : Negative binomial distribution
5893  
5894 Notes
5895 -----
5896 If floating point values are passed for `k` or `n`, they will be truncated
5897 to integers.
5898  
5899 The terms are not summed directly; instead the regularized incomplete beta
5900 function is employed, according to the formula,
5901  
5902 .. math::
5903 \mathrm{nbdtrc}(k, n, p) = I_{1 - p}(k + 1, n).
5904  
5905 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `nbdtrc`.
5906  
5907 The negative binomial distribution is also available as
5908 `scipy.stats.nbinom`. Using `nbdtrc` directly can improve performance
5909 compared to the ``sf`` method of `scipy.stats.nbinom` (see last example).
5910  
5911 References
5912 ----------
5913 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
5914 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
5915  
5916 Examples
5917 --------
5918 Compute the function for ``k=10`` and ``n=5`` at ``p=0.5``.
5919  
5920 >>> import numpy as np
5921 >>> from scipy.special import nbdtrc
5922 >>> nbdtrc(10, 5, 0.5)
5923 0.059234619140624986
5924  
5925 Compute the function for ``n=10`` and ``p=0.5`` at several points by
5926 providing a NumPy array or list for `k`.
5927  
5928 >>> nbdtrc([5, 10, 15], 10, 0.5)
5929 array([0.84912109, 0.41190147, 0.11476147])
5930  
5931 Plot the function for four different parameter sets.
5932  
5933 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
5934 >>> k = np.arange(130)
5935 >>> n_parameters = [20, 20, 20, 80]
5936 >>> p_parameters = [0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.5]
5937 >>> linestyles = ['solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dashdot']
5938 >>> parameters_list = list(zip(p_parameters, n_parameters,
5939 ... linestyles))
5940 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
5941 >>> for parameter_set in parameters_list:
5942 ... p, n, style = parameter_set
5943 ... nbdtrc_vals = nbdtrc(k, n, p)
5944 ... ax.plot(k, nbdtrc_vals, label=rf"$n={n},\, p={p}$",
5945 ... ls=style)
5946 >>> ax.legend()
5947 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$k$")
5948 >>> ax.set_title("Negative binomial distribution survival function")
5949 >>> plt.show()
5950  
5951 The negative binomial distribution is also available as
5952 `scipy.stats.nbinom`. Using `nbdtrc` directly can be much faster than
5953 calling the ``sf`` method of `scipy.stats.nbinom`, especially for small
5954 arrays or individual values. To get the same results one must use the
5955 following parametrization: ``nbinom(n, p).sf(k)=nbdtrc(k, n, p)``.
5956  
5957 >>> from scipy.stats import nbinom
5958 >>> k, n, p = 3, 5, 0.5
5959 >>> nbdtr_res = nbdtrc(k, n, p) # this will often be faster than below
5960 >>> stats_res = nbinom(n, p).sf(k)
5961 >>> stats_res, nbdtr_res # test that results are equal
5962 (0.6367187499999999, 0.6367187499999999)
5963  
5964 `nbdtrc` can evaluate different parameter sets by providing arrays with
5965 shapes compatible for broadcasting for `k`, `n` and `p`. Here we compute
5966 the function for three different `k` at four locations `p`, resulting in
5967 a 3x4 array.
5968  
5969 >>> k = np.array([[5], [10], [15]])
5970 >>> p = np.array([0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9])
5971 >>> k.shape, p.shape
5972 ((3, 1), (4,))
5973  
5974 >>> nbdtrc(k, 5, p)
5975 array([[8.49731667e-01, 3.76953125e-01, 4.73489874e-02, 1.46902600e-04],
5976 [5.15491059e-01, 5.92346191e-02, 6.72234070e-04, 9.29610100e-09],
5977 [2.37507779e-01, 5.90896606e-03, 5.55025308e-06, 3.26346760e-13]])
5978 """)

5981 "nbdtri",
5982 r"""
5983 nbdtri(k, n, y, out=None)
5984  
5985 Returns the inverse with respect to the parameter `p` of
5986 ``y = nbdtr(k, n, p)``, the negative binomial cumulative distribution
5987 function.
5988  
5989 Parameters
5990 ----------
5991 k : array_like
5992 The maximum number of allowed failures (nonnegative int).
5993 n : array_like
5994 The target number of successes (positive int).
5995 y : array_like
5996 The probability of `k` or fewer failures before `n` successes (float).
5997 out : ndarray, optional
5998 Optional output array for the function results
5999  
6000 Returns
6001 -------
6002 p : scalar or ndarray
6003 Probability of success in a single event (float) such that
6004 `nbdtr(k, n, p) = y`.
6005  
6006 See Also
6007 --------
6008 nbdtr : Cumulative distribution function of the negative binomial.
6009 nbdtrc : Negative binomial survival function.
6010 scipy.stats.nbinom : negative binomial distribution.
6011 nbdtrik : Inverse with respect to `k` of `nbdtr(k, n, p)`.
6012 nbdtrin : Inverse with respect to `n` of `nbdtr(k, n, p)`.
6013 scipy.stats.nbinom : Negative binomial distribution
6014  
6015 Notes
6016 -----
6017 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `nbdtri`.
6018  
6019 The negative binomial distribution is also available as
6020 `scipy.stats.nbinom`. Using `nbdtri` directly can improve performance
6021 compared to the ``ppf`` method of `scipy.stats.nbinom`.
6022  
6023 References
6024 ----------
6025 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
6026 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
6027  
6028 Examples
6029 --------
6030 `nbdtri` is the inverse of `nbdtr` with respect to `p`.
6031 Up to floating point errors the following holds:
6032 ``nbdtri(k, n, nbdtr(k, n, p))=p``.
6033  
6034 >>> import numpy as np
6035 >>> from scipy.special import nbdtri, nbdtr
6036 >>> k, n, y = 5, 10, 0.2
6037 >>> cdf_val = nbdtr(k, n, y)
6038 >>> nbdtri(k, n, cdf_val)
6039 0.20000000000000004
6040  
6041 Compute the function for ``k=10`` and ``n=5`` at several points by
6042 providing a NumPy array or list for `y`.
6043  
6044 >>> y = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.8])
6045 >>> nbdtri(3, 5, y)
6046 array([0.34462319, 0.51653095, 0.69677416])
6047  
6048 Plot the function for three different parameter sets.
6049  
6050 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
6051 >>> n_parameters = [5, 20, 30, 30]
6052 >>> k_parameters = [20, 20, 60, 80]
6053 >>> linestyles = ['solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dashdot']
6054 >>> parameters_list = list(zip(n_parameters, k_parameters, linestyles))
6055 >>> cdf_vals = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)
6056 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
6057 >>> for parameter_set in parameters_list:
6058 ... n, k, style = parameter_set
6059 ... nbdtri_vals = nbdtri(k, n, cdf_vals)
6060 ... ax.plot(cdf_vals, nbdtri_vals, label=rf"$k={k},\ n={n}$",
6061 ... ls=style)
6062 >>> ax.legend()
6063 >>> ax.set_ylabel("$p$")
6064 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$CDF$")
6065 >>> title = "nbdtri: inverse of negative binomial CDF with respect to $p$"
6066 >>> ax.set_title(title)
6067 >>> plt.show()
6068  
6069 `nbdtri` can evaluate different parameter sets by providing arrays with
6070 shapes compatible for broadcasting for `k`, `n` and `p`. Here we compute
6071 the function for three different `k` at four locations `p`, resulting in
6072 a 3x4 array.
6073  
6074 >>> k = np.array([[5], [10], [15]])
6075 >>> y = np.array([0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9])
6076 >>> k.shape, y.shape
6077 ((3, 1), (4,))
6078  
6079 >>> nbdtri(k, 5, y)
6080 array([[0.37258157, 0.45169416, 0.53249956, 0.64578407],
6081 [0.24588501, 0.30451981, 0.36778453, 0.46397088],
6082 [0.18362101, 0.22966758, 0.28054743, 0.36066188]])
6083 """)

6085 add_newdoc("nbdtrik",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
6086 r"""
6087 nbdtrik(y, n, p, out=None)
6088  
6089 Negative binomial percentile function.
6090  
6091 Returns the inverse with respect to the parameter `k` of
6092 ``y = nbdtr(k, n, p)``, the negative binomial cumulative distribution
6093 function.
6094  
6095 Parameters
6096 ----------
6097 y : array_like
6098 The probability of `k` or fewer failures before `n` successes (float).
6099 n : array_like
6100 The target number of successes (positive int).
6101 p : array_like
6102 Probability of success in a single event (float).
6103 out : ndarray, optional
6104 Optional output array for the function results
6105  
6106 Returns
6107 -------
6108 k : scalar or ndarray
6109 The maximum number of allowed failures such that `nbdtr(k, n, p) = y`.
6110  
6111 See Also
6112 --------
6113 nbdtr : Cumulative distribution function of the negative binomial.
6114 nbdtrc : Survival function of the negative binomial.
6115 nbdtri : Inverse with respect to `p` of `nbdtr(k, n, p)`.
6116 nbdtrin : Inverse with respect to `n` of `nbdtr(k, n, p)`.
6117 scipy.stats.nbinom : Negative binomial distribution
6118  
6119 Notes
6120 -----
6121 Wrapper for the CDFLIB [1]_ Fortran routine `cdfnbn`.
6122  
6123 Formula 26.5.26 of [2]_,
6124  
6125 .. math::
6126 \sum_{j=k + 1}^\infty {{n + j - 1}
6127 \choose{j}} p^n (1 - p)^j = I_{1 - p}(k + 1, n),
6128  
6129 is used to reduce calculation of the cumulative distribution function to
6130 that of a regularized incomplete beta :math:`I`.
6131  
6132 Computation of `k` involves a search for a value that produces the desired
6133 value of `y`. The search relies on the monotonicity of `y` with `k`.
6134  
6135 References
6136 ----------
6137 .. [1] Barry Brown, James Lovato, and Kathy Russell,
6138 CDFLIB: Library of Fortran Routines for Cumulative Distribution
6139 Functions, Inverses, and Other Parameters.
6140 .. [2] Milton Abramowitz and Irene A. Stegun, eds.
6141 Handbook of Mathematical Functions with Formulas,
6142 Graphs, and Mathematical Tables. New York: Dover, 1972.
6143  
6144 Examples
6145 --------
6146 Compute the negative binomial cumulative distribution function for an
6147 exemplary parameter set.
6148  
6149 >>> import numpy as np
6150 >>> from scipy.special import nbdtr, nbdtrik
6151 >>> k, n, p = 5, 2, 0.5
6152 >>> cdf_value = nbdtr(k, n, p)
6153 >>> cdf_value
6154 0.9375
6155  
6156 Verify that `nbdtrik` recovers the original value for `k`.
6157  
6158 >>> nbdtrik(cdf_value, n, p)
6159 5.0
6160  
6161 Plot the function for different parameter sets.
6162  
6163 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
6164 >>> p_parameters = [0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 0.5]
6165 >>> n_parameters = [30, 30, 30, 80]
6166 >>> linestyles = ['solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dashdot']
6167 >>> parameters_list = list(zip(p_parameters, n_parameters, linestyles))
6168 >>> cdf_vals = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)
6169 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
6170 >>> for parameter_set in parameters_list:
6171 ... p, n, style = parameter_set
6172 ... nbdtrik_vals = nbdtrik(cdf_vals, n, p)
6173 ... ax.plot(cdf_vals, nbdtrik_vals, label=rf"$n={n},\ p={p}$",
6174 ... ls=style)
6175 >>> ax.legend()
6176 >>> ax.set_ylabel("$k$")
6177 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$CDF$")
6178 >>> ax.set_title("Negative binomial percentile function")
6179 >>> plt.show()
6180  
6181 The negative binomial distribution is also available as
6182 `scipy.stats.nbinom`. The percentile function method ``ppf``
6183 returns the result of `nbdtrik` rounded up to integers:
6184  
6185 >>> from scipy.stats import nbinom
6186 >>> q, n, p = 0.6, 5, 0.5
6187 >>> nbinom.ppf(q, n, p), nbdtrik(q, n, p)
6188 (5.0, 4.800428460273882)
6189  
6190 """)

6192 add_newdoc("nbdtrin",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
6193 r"""
6194 nbdtrin(k, y, p, out=None)
6195  
6196 Inverse of `nbdtr` vs `n`.
6197  
6198 Returns the inverse with respect to the parameter `n` of
6199 ``y = nbdtr(k, n, p)``, the negative binomial cumulative distribution
6200 function.
6201  
6202 Parameters
6203 ----------
6204 k : array_like
6205 The maximum number of allowed failures (nonnegative int).
6206 y : array_like
6207 The probability of `k` or fewer failures before `n` successes (float).
6208 p : array_like
6209 Probability of success in a single event (float).
6210 out : ndarray, optional
6211 Optional output array for the function results
6212  
6213 Returns
6214 -------
6215 n : scalar or ndarray
6216 The number of successes `n` such that `nbdtr(k, n, p) = y`.
6217  
6218 See Also
6219 --------
6220 nbdtr : Cumulative distribution function of the negative binomial.
6221 nbdtri : Inverse with respect to `p` of `nbdtr(k, n, p)`.
6222 nbdtrik : Inverse with respect to `k` of `nbdtr(k, n, p)`.
6223  
6224 Notes
6225 -----
6226 Wrapper for the CDFLIB [1]_ Fortran routine `cdfnbn`.
6227  
6228 Formula 26.5.26 of [2]_,
6229  
6230 .. math::
6231 \sum_{j=k + 1}^\infty {{n + j - 1}
6232 \choose{j}} p^n (1 - p)^j = I_{1 - p}(k + 1, n),
6233  
6234 is used to reduce calculation of the cumulative distribution function to
6235 that of a regularized incomplete beta :math:`I`.
6236  
6237 Computation of `n` involves a search for a value that produces the desired
6238 value of `y`. The search relies on the monotonicity of `y` with `n`.
6239  
6240 References
6241 ----------
6242 .. [1] Barry Brown, James Lovato, and Kathy Russell,
6243 CDFLIB: Library of Fortran Routines for Cumulative Distribution
6244 Functions, Inverses, and Other Parameters.
6245 .. [2] Milton Abramowitz and Irene A. Stegun, eds.
6246 Handbook of Mathematical Functions with Formulas,
6247 Graphs, and Mathematical Tables. New York: Dover, 1972.
6248  
6249 Examples
6250 --------
6251 Compute the negative binomial cumulative distribution function for an
6252 exemplary parameter set.
6253  
6254 >>> from scipy.special import nbdtr, nbdtrin
6255 >>> k, n, p = 5, 2, 0.5
6256 >>> cdf_value = nbdtr(k, n, p)
6257 >>> cdf_value
6258 0.9375
6259  
6260 Verify that `nbdtrin` recovers the original value for `n` up to floating
6261 point accuracy.
6262  
6263 >>> nbdtrin(k, cdf_value, p)
6264 1.999999999998137
6265 """)

6268 r"""
6269 ncfdtr(dfn, dfd, nc, f, out=None)
6270  
6271 Cumulative distribution function of the non-central F distribution.
6272  
6273 The non-central F describes the distribution of,
6274  
6275 .. math::
6276 Z = \frac{X/d_n}{Y/d_d}
6277  
6278 where :math:`X` and :math:`Y` are independently distributed, with
6279 :math:`X` distributed non-central :math:`\chi^2` with noncentrality
6280 parameter `nc` and :math:`d_n` degrees of freedom, and :math:`Y`
6281 distributed :math:`\chi^2` with :math:`d_d` degrees of freedom.
6282  
6283 Parameters
6284 ----------
6285 dfn : array_like
6286 Degrees of freedom of the numerator sum of squares. Range (0, inf).
6287 dfd : array_like
6288 Degrees of freedom of the denominator sum of squares. Range (0, inf).
6289 nc : array_like
6290 Noncentrality parameter. Range [0, inf).
6291 f : array_like
6292 Quantiles, i.e. the upper limit of integration.
6293 out : ndarray, optional
6294 Optional output array for the function results
6295  
6296 Returns
6297 -------
6298 cdf : scalar or ndarray
6299 The calculated CDF. If all inputs are scalar, the return will be a
6300 float. Otherwise it will be an array.
6301  
6302 See Also
6303 --------
6304 ncfdtri : Quantile function; inverse of `ncfdtr` with respect to `f`.
6305 ncfdtridfd : Inverse of `ncfdtr` with respect to `dfd`.
6306 ncfdtridfn : Inverse of `ncfdtr` with respect to `dfn`.
6307 ncfdtrinc : Inverse of `ncfdtr` with respect to `nc`.
6308 scipy.stats.ncf : Non-central F distribution.
6309  
6310 Notes
6311 -----
6312 This function calculates the CDF of the non-central f distribution using
6313 the Boost Math C++ library [1]_.
6314  
6315 The cumulative distribution function is computed using Formula 26.6.20 of
6316 [2]_:
6317  
6318 .. math::
6319 F(d_n, d_d, n_c, f) = \sum_{j=0}^\infty e^{-n_c/2}
6320 \frac{(n_c/2)^j}{j!} I_{x}(\frac{d_n}{2} + j, \frac{d_d}{2}),
6321  
6322 where :math:`I` is the regularized incomplete beta function, and
6323 :math:`x = f d_n/(f d_n + d_d)`.
6324  
6325 Note that argument order of `ncfdtr` is different from that of the
6326 similar ``cdf`` method of `scipy.stats.ncf`: `f` is the last
6327 parameter of `ncfdtr` but the first parameter of ``scipy.stats.ncf.cdf``.
6328  
6329 References
6330 ----------
6331 .. [1] The Boost Developers. "Boost C++ Libraries". https://www.boost.org/.
6332 .. [2] Milton Abramowitz and Irene A. Stegun, eds.
6333 Handbook of Mathematical Functions with Formulas,
6334 Graphs, and Mathematical Tables. New York: Dover, 1972.
6335  
6336 Examples
6337 --------
6338 >>> import numpy as np
6339 >>> from scipy import special
6340 >>> from scipy import stats
6341 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
6342  
6343 Plot the CDF of the non-central F distribution, for nc=0. Compare with the
6344 F-distribution from scipy.stats:
6345  
6346 >>> x = np.linspace(-1, 8, num=500)
6347 >>> dfn = 3
6348 >>> dfd = 2
6349 >>> ncf_stats = stats.f.cdf(x, dfn, dfd)
6350 >>> ncf_special = special.ncfdtr(dfn, dfd, 0, x)
6351  
6352 >>> fig = plt.figure()
6353 >>> ax = fig.add_subplot(111)
6354 >>> ax.plot(x, ncf_stats, 'b-', lw=3)
6355 >>> ax.plot(x, ncf_special, 'r-')
6356 >>> plt.show()
6357  
6358 """)
6359

6851  
6852 Examples
6853 --------
6854 `nrdtrimn` can be used to recover the mean of a normal distribution
6855 if we know the CDF value `p` for a given quantile `x` and the
6856 standard deviation `std`. First, we calculate
6857 the normal distribution CDF for an exemplary parameter set.
6858  
6859 >>> from scipy.stats import norm
6860 >>> mean = 3.
6861 >>> std = 2.
6862 >>> x = 6.

6985 r"""
6986 pdtr(k, m, out=None)
6987  
6988 Poisson cumulative distribution function.
6989  
6990 Defined as the probability that a Poisson-distributed random
6991 variable with event rate :math:`m` is less than or equal to
6992 :math:`k`. More concretely, this works out to be [1]_
6993  
6994 .. math::
6995  
6996 \exp(-m) \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor{k}\rfloor} \frac{m^j}{j!}.
6997  
6998 Parameters
6999 ----------
7000 k : array_like
7001 Number of occurrences (nonnegative, real)
7002 m : array_like
7003 Shape parameter (nonnegative, real)
7004 out : ndarray, optional
7005 Optional output array for the function results
7006  
7007 Returns
7008 -------
7009 scalar or ndarray
7010 Values of the Poisson cumulative distribution function
7011  
7012 See Also
7013 --------
7014 pdtrc : Poisson survival function
7015 pdtrik : inverse of `pdtr` with respect to `k`
7016 pdtri : inverse of `pdtr` with respect to `m`
7017  
7018 References
7019 ----------
7020 .. [1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution
7021  
7022 Examples
7023 --------
7024 >>> import numpy as np
7025 >>> import scipy.special as sc
7026  
7027 It is a cumulative distribution function, so it converges to 1
7028 monotonically as `k` goes to infinity.
7029  
7030 >>> sc.pdtr([1, 10, 100, np.inf], 1)
7031 array([0.73575888, 0.99999999, 1. , 1. ])
7032  
7033 It is discontinuous at integers and constant between integers.
7034  
7035 >>> sc.pdtr([1, 1.5, 1.9, 2], 1)
7036 array([0.73575888, 0.73575888, 0.73575888, 0.9196986 ])
7037  
7038 """)

7041 """
7042 pdtrc(k, m, out=None)
7043  
7044 Poisson survival function
7045  
7046 Returns the sum of the terms from k+1 to infinity of the Poisson
7047 distribution: sum(exp(-m) * m**j / j!, j=k+1..inf) = gammainc(
7048 k+1, m). Arguments must both be non-negative doubles.
7049  
7050 Parameters
7051 ----------
7052 k : array_like
7053 Number of occurrences (nonnegative, real)
7054 m : array_like
7055 Shape parameter (nonnegative, real)
7056 out : ndarray, optional
7057 Optional output array for the function results
7058  
7059 Returns
7060 -------
7061 scalar or ndarray
7062 Values of the Poisson survival function
7063  
7064 See Also
7065 --------
7066 pdtr : Poisson cumulative distribution function
7067 pdtrik : inverse of `pdtr` with respect to `k`
7068 pdtri : inverse of `pdtr` with respect to `m`
7069  
7070 Examples
7071 --------
7072 >>> import numpy as np
7073 >>> import scipy.special as sc
7074  
7075 It is a survival function, so it decreases to 0
7076 monotonically as `k` goes to infinity.
7077  
7078 >>> k = np.array([1, 10, 100, np.inf])
7079 >>> sc.pdtrc(k, 1)
7080 array([2.64241118e-001, 1.00477664e-008, 3.94147589e-161, 0.00000000e+000])
7081  
7082 It can be expressed in terms of the lower incomplete gamma
7083 function `gammainc`.
7084  
7085 >>> sc.gammainc(k + 1, 1)
7086 array([2.64241118e-001, 1.00477664e-008, 3.94147589e-161, 0.00000000e+000])
7087  
7088 """)

7092 pdtri(k, y, out=None)
7093  
7094 Inverse to `pdtr` vs m
7095  
7096 Returns the Poisson variable `m` such that the sum from 0 to `k` of
7097 the Poisson density is equal to the given probability `y`:
7098 calculated by ``gammaincinv(k + 1, y)``. `k` must be a nonnegative
7099 integer and `y` between 0 and 1.
7100  
7101 Parameters
7102 ----------
7103 k : array_like
7104 Number of occurrences (nonnegative, real)
7105 y : array_like
7106 Probability
7107 out : ndarray, optional
7108 Optional output array for the function results
7109  
7110 Returns
7111 -------
7112 scalar or ndarray
7113 Values of the shape parameter `m` such that ``pdtr(k, m) = p``
7114  
7115 See Also
7116 --------
7117 pdtr : Poisson cumulative distribution function
7118 pdtrc : Poisson survival function
7119 pdtrik : inverse of `pdtr` with respect to `k`

7122 --------
7123 >>> import scipy.special as sc
7124  
7125 Compute the CDF for several values of `m`:

7129 >>> p
7130 array([0.90979599, 0.73575888, 0.5578254 ])
7131  
7132 Compute the inverse. We recover the values of `m`, as expected:
7133

7184 r"""
7185 poch(z, m, out=None)
7186  
7187 Pochhammer symbol.
7188  
7189 The Pochhammer symbol (rising factorial) is defined as
7190  
7191 .. math::
7192  
7193 (z)_m = \frac{\Gamma(z + m)}{\Gamma(z)}
7194  
7195 For positive integer `m` it reads
7196  
7197 .. math::
7198  
7199 (z)_m = z (z + 1) ... (z + m - 1)
7200  
7201 See [dlmf]_ for more details.
7202  
7203 Parameters
7204 ----------
7205 z, m : array_like
7206 Real-valued arguments.
7207 out : ndarray, optional
7208 Optional output array for the function results
7209  
7210 Returns
7211 -------
7212 scalar or ndarray
7213 The value of the function.
7214  
7215 References
7216 ----------
7217 .. [dlmf] Nist, Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
7218 https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2#iii
7219  
7220 Examples
7221 --------
7222 >>> import scipy.special as sc
7223  
7224 It is 1 when m is 0.
7225  
7226 >>> sc.poch([1, 2, 3, 4], 0)
7227 array([1., 1., 1., 1.])
7228  
7229 For z equal to 1 it reduces to the factorial function.
7230  
7231 >>> sc.poch(1, 5)
7232 120.0
7233 >>> 1 * 2 * 3 * 4 * 5
7234 120
7235  
7236 It can be expressed in terms of the gamma function.
7237  
7238 >>> z, m = 3.7, 2.1
7239 >>> sc.poch(z, m)
7240 20.529581933776953
7241 >>> sc.gamma(z + m) / sc.gamma(z)
7242 20.52958193377696
7243  
7244 """)

7246 add_newdoc("powm1", """
7247 powm1(x, y, out=None)
7248  
7249 Computes ``x**y - 1``.
7250  
7251 This function is useful when `y` is near 0, or when `x` is near 1.
7252  
7253 The function is implemented for real types only (unlike ``numpy.power``,
7254 which accepts complex inputs).
7255  
7256 Parameters
7257 ----------
7258 x : array_like
7259 The base. Must be a real type (i.e. integer or float, not complex).
7260 y : array_like
7261 The exponent. Must be a real type (i.e. integer or float, not complex).
7262  
7263 Returns
7264 -------
7265 array_like
7266 Result of the calculation
7267  
7268 Notes
7269 -----
7270 .. versionadded:: 1.10.0
7271  
7272 The underlying code is implemented for single precision and double
7273 precision floats only. Unlike `numpy.power`, integer inputs to
7274 `powm1` are converted to floating point, and complex inputs are
7275 not accepted.
7276  
7277 Note the following edge cases:
7278  
7279 * ``powm1(x, 0)`` returns 0 for any ``x``, including 0, ``inf``
7280 and ``nan``.
7281 * ``powm1(1, y)`` returns 0 for any ``y``, including ``nan``
7282 and ``inf``.
7283  
7284 This function wraps the ``powm1`` routine from the
7285 Boost Math C++ library [1]_.
7286  
7287 References
7288 ----------
7289 .. [1] The Boost Developers. "Boost C++ Libraries". https://www.boost.org/.
7290  
7291 Examples
7292 --------
7293 >>> import numpy as np
7294 >>> from scipy.special import powm1
7295  
7296 >>> x = np.array([1.2, 10.0, 0.9999999975])
7297 >>> y = np.array([1e-9, 1e-11, 0.1875])
7298 >>> powm1(x, y)
7299 array([ 1.82321557e-10, 2.30258509e-11, -4.68749998e-10])
7300  
7301 It can be verified that the relative errors in those results
7302 are less than 2.5e-16.
7303  
7304 Compare that to the result of ``x**y - 1``, where the
7305 relative errors are all larger than 8e-8:
7306  
7307 >>> x**y - 1
7308 array([ 1.82321491e-10, 2.30258035e-11, -4.68750039e-10])
7309  
7310 """)

7313 add_newdoc("pseudo_huber",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
7314 r"""
7315 pseudo_huber(delta, r, out=None)
7316  
7317 Pseudo-Huber loss function.
7318  
7319 .. math:: \mathrm{pseudo\_huber}(\delta, r) =
  • E501 Line too long (88 > 79 characters)
7320 \delta^2 \left( \sqrt{ 1 + \left( \frac{r}{\delta} \right)^2 } - 1 \right)
7321  
7322 Parameters
7323 ----------
7324 delta : array_like
7325 Input array, indicating the soft quadratic vs. linear loss changepoint.
7326 r : array_like
7327 Input array, possibly representing residuals.
7328 out : ndarray, optional
7329 Optional output array for the function results
7330  
7331 Returns
7332 -------
7333 res : scalar or ndarray
7334 The computed Pseudo-Huber loss function values.
7335  
7336 See Also
7337 --------
7338 huber: Similar function which this function approximates
7339  
7340 Notes
7341 -----
7342 Like `huber`, `pseudo_huber` often serves as a robust loss function
7343 in statistics or machine learning to reduce the influence of outliers.
7344 Unlike `huber`, `pseudo_huber` is smooth.
7345  
7346 Typically, `r` represents residuals, the difference
7347 between a model prediction and data. Then, for :math:`|r|\leq\delta`,
7348 `pseudo_huber` resembles the squared error and for :math:`|r|>\delta` the
7349 absolute error. This way, the Pseudo-Huber loss often achieves
7350 a fast convergence in model fitting for small residuals like the squared
7351 error loss function and still reduces the influence of outliers
7352 (:math:`|r|>\delta`) like the absolute error loss. As :math:`\delta` is
7353 the cutoff between squared and absolute error regimes, it has
7354 to be tuned carefully for each problem. `pseudo_huber` is also
7355 convex, making it suitable for gradient based optimization. [1]_ [2]_
7356  
7357 .. versionadded:: 0.15.0
7358  
7359 References
7360 ----------
7361 .. [1] Hartley, Zisserman, "Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision".
7362 2003. Cambridge University Press. p. 619
7363 .. [2] Charbonnier et al. "Deterministic edge-preserving regularization
7364 in computed imaging". 1997. IEEE Trans. Image Processing.
7365 6 (2): 298 - 311.
7366  
7367 Examples
7368 --------
7369 Import all necessary modules.
7370  
7371 >>> import numpy as np
7372 >>> from scipy.special import pseudo_huber, huber
7373 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
7374  
7375 Calculate the function for ``delta=1`` at ``r=2``.
7376  
7377 >>> pseudo_huber(1., 2.)
7378 1.2360679774997898
7379  
7380 Calculate the function at ``r=2`` for different `delta` by providing
7381 a list or NumPy array for `delta`.
7382  
7383 >>> pseudo_huber([1., 2., 4.], 3.)
7384 array([2.16227766, 3.21110255, 4. ])
7385  
7386 Calculate the function for ``delta=1`` at several points by providing
7387 a list or NumPy array for `r`.
7388  
7389 >>> pseudo_huber(2., np.array([1., 1.5, 3., 4.]))
7390 array([0.47213595, 1. , 3.21110255, 4.94427191])
7391  
7392 The function can be calculated for different `delta` and `r` by
7393 providing arrays for both with compatible shapes for broadcasting.
7394  
7395 >>> r = np.array([1., 2.5, 8., 10.])
7396 >>> deltas = np.array([[1.], [5.], [9.]])
7397 >>> print(r.shape, deltas.shape)
7398 (4,) (3, 1)
7399  
7400 >>> pseudo_huber(deltas, r)
7401 array([[ 0.41421356, 1.6925824 , 7.06225775, 9.04987562],
7402 [ 0.49509757, 2.95084972, 22.16990566, 30.90169944],
7403 [ 0.49846624, 3.06693762, 27.37435121, 40.08261642]])
7404  
7405 Plot the function for different `delta`.
7406  
7407 >>> x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 500)
7408 >>> deltas = [1, 2, 3]
7409 >>> linestyles = ["dashed", "dotted", "dashdot"]
7410 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
7411 >>> combined_plot_parameters = list(zip(deltas, linestyles))
7412 >>> for delta, style in combined_plot_parameters:
7413 ... ax.plot(x, pseudo_huber(delta, x), label=rf"$\delta={delta}$",
7414 ... ls=style)
7415 >>> ax.legend(loc="upper center")
7416 >>> ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
7417 >>> ax.set_title(r"Pseudo-Huber loss function $h_{\delta}(x)$")
7418 >>> ax.set_xlim(-4, 4)
7419 >>> ax.set_ylim(0, 8)
7420 >>> plt.show()
7421  
7422 Finally, illustrate the difference between `huber` and `pseudo_huber` by
7423 plotting them and their gradients with respect to `r`. The plot shows
7424 that `pseudo_huber` is continuously differentiable while `huber` is not
7425 at the points :math:`\pm\delta`.
7426  
7427 >>> def huber_grad(delta, x):
7428 ... grad = np.copy(x)
7429 ... linear_area = np.argwhere(np.abs(x) > delta)
7430 ... grad[linear_area]=delta*np.sign(x[linear_area])
7431 ... return grad
7432 >>> def pseudo_huber_grad(delta, x):
7433 ... return x* (1+(x/delta)**2)**(-0.5)
7434 >>> x=np.linspace(-3, 3, 500)
7435 >>> delta = 1.
7436 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
7437 >>> ax.plot(x, huber(delta, x), label="Huber", ls="dashed")
7438 >>> ax.plot(x, huber_grad(delta, x), label="Huber Gradient", ls="dashdot")
7439 >>> ax.plot(x, pseudo_huber(delta, x), label="Pseudo-Huber", ls="dotted")
7440 >>> ax.plot(x, pseudo_huber_grad(delta, x), label="Pseudo-Huber Gradient",
7441 ... ls="solid")
7442 >>> ax.legend(loc="upper center")
7443 >>> plt.show()
7444 """)
7445

  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
7447 r"""
7448 rel_entr(x, y, out=None)
7449  
7450 Elementwise function for computing relative entropy.
7451  
7452 .. math::
7453  
7454 \mathrm{rel\_entr}(x, y) =
7455 \begin{cases}
7456 x \log(x / y) & x > 0, y > 0 \\
7457 0 & x = 0, y \ge 0 \\
7458 \infty & \text{otherwise}
7459 \end{cases}
7460  
7461 Parameters
7462 ----------
7463 x, y : array_like
7464 Input arrays
7465 out : ndarray, optional
7466 Optional output array for the function results
7467  
7468 Returns
7469 -------
7470 scalar or ndarray
7471 Relative entropy of the inputs
7472  
7473 See Also
7474 --------
7475 entr, kl_div, scipy.stats.entropy
7476  
7477 Notes
7478 -----
7479 .. versionadded:: 0.15.0
7480  
7481 This function is jointly convex in x and y.
7482  
7483 The origin of this function is in convex programming; see
7484 [1]_. Given two discrete probability distributions :math:`p_1,
7485 \ldots, p_n` and :math:`q_1, \ldots, q_n`, the definition of relative
7486 entropy in the context of *information theory* is
7487  
7488 .. math::
7489  
7490 \sum_{i = 1}^n \mathrm{rel\_entr}(p_i, q_i).
7491  
7492 To compute the latter quantity, use `scipy.stats.entropy`.
7493  
7494 See [2]_ for details.
7495  
7496 References
7497 ----------
7498 .. [1] Boyd, Stephen and Lieven Vandenberghe. *Convex optimization*.
7499 Cambridge University Press, 2004.
7500 :doi:`https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804441`
7501 .. [2] Kullback-Leibler divergence,
7502 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence
7503  
7504 """)

7539 add_newdoc("shichi",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
7540 r"""
7541 shichi(x, out=None)
7542  
7543 Hyperbolic sine and cosine integrals.
7544  
7545 The hyperbolic sine integral is
7546  
7547 .. math::
7548  
7549 \int_0^x \frac{\sinh{t}}{t}dt
7550  
7551 and the hyperbolic cosine integral is
7552  
7553 .. math::
7554  
7555 \gamma + \log(x) + \int_0^x \frac{\cosh{t} - 1}{t} dt
7556  
7557 where :math:`\gamma` is Euler's constant and :math:`\log` is the
7558 principal branch of the logarithm [1]_.
7559  
7560 Parameters
7561 ----------
7562 x : array_like
7563 Real or complex points at which to compute the hyperbolic sine
7564 and cosine integrals.
7565 out : tuple of ndarray, optional
7566 Optional output arrays for the function results
7567  
7568 Returns
7569 -------
7570 si : scalar or ndarray
7571 Hyperbolic sine integral at ``x``
7572 ci : scalar or ndarray
7573 Hyperbolic cosine integral at ``x``
7574  
7575 See Also
7576 --------
7577 sici : Sine and cosine integrals.
7578 exp1 : Exponential integral E1.
7579 expi : Exponential integral Ei.
7580  
7581 Notes
7582 -----
7583 For real arguments with ``x < 0``, ``chi`` is the real part of the
7584 hyperbolic cosine integral. For such points ``chi(x)`` and ``chi(x
7585 + 0j)`` differ by a factor of ``1j*pi``.
7586  
7587 For real arguments the function is computed by calling Cephes'
7588 [2]_ *shichi* routine. For complex arguments the algorithm is based
7589 on Mpmath's [3]_ *shi* and *chi* routines.
7590  
7591 References
7592 ----------
7593 .. [1] Milton Abramowitz and Irene A. Stegun, eds.
7594 Handbook of Mathematical Functions with Formulas,
7595 Graphs, and Mathematical Tables. New York: Dover, 1972.
7596 (See Section 5.2.)
7597 .. [2] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
7598 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
7599 .. [3] Fredrik Johansson and others.
7600 "mpmath: a Python library for arbitrary-precision floating-point
7601 arithmetic" (Version 0.19) http://mpmath.org/
7602  
7603 Examples
7604 --------
7605 >>> import numpy as np
7606 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
7607 >>> from scipy.special import shichi, sici
7608  
7609 `shichi` accepts real or complex input:
7610  
7611 >>> shichi(0.5)
7612 (0.5069967498196671, -0.05277684495649357)
7613 >>> shichi(0.5 + 2.5j)
7614 ((0.11772029666668238+1.831091777729851j),
7615 (0.29912435887648825+1.7395351121166562j))
7616  
7617 The hyperbolic sine and cosine integrals Shi(z) and Chi(z) are
7618 related to the sine and cosine integrals Si(z) and Ci(z) by
7619  
7620 * Shi(z) = -i*Si(i*z)
7621 * Chi(z) = Ci(-i*z) + i*pi/2
7622  
7623 >>> z = 0.25 + 5j
7624 >>> shi, chi = shichi(z)
7625 >>> shi, -1j*sici(1j*z)[0] # Should be the same.
7626 ((-0.04834719325101729+1.5469354086921228j),
7627 (-0.04834719325101729+1.5469354086921228j))
7628 >>> chi, sici(-1j*z)[1] + 1j*np.pi/2 # Should be the same.
7629 ((-0.19568708973868087+1.556276312103824j),
7630 (-0.19568708973868087+1.556276312103824j))
7631  
7632 Plot the functions evaluated on the real axis:
7633  
7634 >>> xp = np.geomspace(1e-8, 4.0, 250)
7635 >>> x = np.concatenate((-xp[::-1], xp))
7636 >>> shi, chi = shichi(x)
7637  
7638 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
7639 >>> ax.plot(x, shi, label='Shi(x)')
7640 >>> ax.plot(x, chi, '--', label='Chi(x)')
7641 >>> ax.set_xlabel('x')
7642 >>> ax.set_title('Hyperbolic Sine and Cosine Integrals')
7643 >>> ax.legend(shadow=True, framealpha=1, loc='lower right')
7644 >>> ax.grid(True)
7645 >>> plt.show()
7646  
7647 """)

7649 add_newdoc("sici",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
7650 r"""
7651 sici(x, out=None)
7652  
7653 Sine and cosine integrals.
7654  
7655 The sine integral is
7656  
7657 .. math::
7658  
7659 \int_0^x \frac{\sin{t}}{t}dt
7660  
7661 and the cosine integral is
7662  
7663 .. math::
7664  
7665 \gamma + \log(x) + \int_0^x \frac{\cos{t} - 1}{t}dt
7666  
7667 where :math:`\gamma` is Euler's constant and :math:`\log` is the
7668 principal branch of the logarithm [1]_.
7669  
7670 Parameters
7671 ----------
7672 x : array_like
7673 Real or complex points at which to compute the sine and cosine
7674 integrals.
7675 out : tuple of ndarray, optional
7676 Optional output arrays for the function results
7677  
7678 Returns
7679 -------
7680 si : scalar or ndarray
7681 Sine integral at ``x``
7682 ci : scalar or ndarray
7683 Cosine integral at ``x``
7684  
7685 See Also
7686 --------
7687 shichi : Hyperbolic sine and cosine integrals.
7688 exp1 : Exponential integral E1.
7689 expi : Exponential integral Ei.
7690  
7691 Notes
7692 -----
7693 For real arguments with ``x < 0``, ``ci`` is the real part of the
7694 cosine integral. For such points ``ci(x)`` and ``ci(x + 0j)``
7695 differ by a factor of ``1j*pi``.
7696  
7697 For real arguments the function is computed by calling Cephes'
7698 [2]_ *sici* routine. For complex arguments the algorithm is based
7699 on Mpmath's [3]_ *si* and *ci* routines.
7700  
7701 References
7702 ----------
7703 .. [1] Milton Abramowitz and Irene A. Stegun, eds.
7704 Handbook of Mathematical Functions with Formulas,
7705 Graphs, and Mathematical Tables. New York: Dover, 1972.
7706 (See Section 5.2.)
7707 .. [2] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
7708 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
7709 .. [3] Fredrik Johansson and others.
7710 "mpmath: a Python library for arbitrary-precision floating-point
7711 arithmetic" (Version 0.19) http://mpmath.org/
7712  
7713 Examples
7714 --------
7715 >>> import numpy as np
7716 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
7717 >>> from scipy.special import sici, exp1
7718  
7719 `sici` accepts real or complex input:
7720  
7721 >>> sici(2.5)
7722 (1.7785201734438267, 0.2858711963653835)
7723 >>> sici(2.5 + 3j)
7724 ((4.505735874563953+0.06863305018999577j),
7725 (0.0793644206906966-2.935510262937543j))
7726  
7727 For z in the right half plane, the sine and cosine integrals are
7728 related to the exponential integral E1 (implemented in SciPy as
7729 `scipy.special.exp1`) by
7730  
7731 * Si(z) = (E1(i*z) - E1(-i*z))/2i + pi/2
7732 * Ci(z) = -(E1(i*z) + E1(-i*z))/2
7733  
7734 See [1]_ (equations 5.2.21 and 5.2.23).
7735  
7736 We can verify these relations:
7737  
7738 >>> z = 2 - 3j
7739 >>> sici(z)
7740 ((4.54751388956229-1.3991965806460565j),
7741 (1.408292501520851+2.9836177420296055j))
7742  
7743 >>> (exp1(1j*z) - exp1(-1j*z))/2j + np.pi/2 # Same as sine integral
7744 (4.54751388956229-1.3991965806460565j)
7745  
7746 >>> -(exp1(1j*z) + exp1(-1j*z))/2 # Same as cosine integral
7747 (1.408292501520851+2.9836177420296055j)
7748  
7749 Plot the functions evaluated on the real axis; the dotted horizontal
7750 lines are at pi/2 and -pi/2:
7751  
7752 >>> x = np.linspace(-16, 16, 150)
7753 >>> si, ci = sici(x)
7754  
7755 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
7756 >>> ax.plot(x, si, label='Si(x)')
7757 >>> ax.plot(x, ci, '--', label='Ci(x)')
7758 >>> ax.legend(shadow=True, framealpha=1, loc='upper left')
7759 >>> ax.set_xlabel('x')
7760 >>> ax.set_title('Sine and Cosine Integrals')
7761 >>> ax.axhline(np.pi/2, linestyle=':', alpha=0.5, color='k')
7762 >>> ax.axhline(-np.pi/2, linestyle=':', alpha=0.5, color='k')
7763 >>> ax.grid(True)
7764 >>> plt.show()
7765  
7766 """)

7768 add_newdoc("smirnov",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
7769 r"""
7770 smirnov(n, d, out=None)
7771  
7772 Kolmogorov-Smirnov complementary cumulative distribution function
7773  
7774 Returns the exact Kolmogorov-Smirnov complementary cumulative
7775 distribution function,(aka the Survival Function) of Dn+ (or Dn-)
7776 for a one-sided test of equality between an empirical and a
7777 theoretical distribution. It is equal to the probability that the
7778 maximum difference between a theoretical distribution and an empirical
7779 one based on `n` samples is greater than d.
7780  
7781 Parameters
7782 ----------
7783 n : int
7784 Number of samples
7785 d : float array_like
7786 Deviation between the Empirical CDF (ECDF) and the target CDF.
7787 out : ndarray, optional
7788 Optional output array for the function results
7789  
7790 Returns
7791 -------
7792 scalar or ndarray
7793 The value(s) of smirnov(n, d), Prob(Dn+ >= d) (Also Prob(Dn- >= d))
7794  
7795 See Also
7796 --------
7797 smirnovi : The Inverse Survival Function for the distribution
7798 scipy.stats.ksone : Provides the functionality as a continuous distribution
7799 kolmogorov, kolmogi : Functions for the two-sided distribution
7800  
7801 Notes
7802 -----
7803 `smirnov` is used by `stats.kstest` in the application of the
7804 Kolmogorov-Smirnov Goodness of Fit test. For historical reasons this
7805 function is exposed in `scpy.special`, but the recommended way to achieve
7806 the most accurate CDF/SF/PDF/PPF/ISF computations is to use the
7807 `stats.ksone` distribution.
7808  
7809 Examples
7810 --------
7811 >>> import numpy as np
7812 >>> from scipy.special import smirnov
7813 >>> from scipy.stats import norm
7814  
7815 Show the probability of a gap at least as big as 0, 0.5 and 1.0 for a
7816 sample of size 5.
7817  
7818 >>> smirnov(5, [0, 0.5, 1.0])
7819 array([ 1. , 0.056, 0. ])
7820  
7821 Compare a sample of size 5 against N(0, 1), the standard normal
7822 distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
7823  
7824 `x` is the sample.
7825  
7826 >>> x = np.array([-1.392, -0.135, 0.114, 0.190, 1.82])
7827  
7828 >>> target = norm(0, 1)
7829 >>> cdfs = target.cdf(x)
7830 >>> cdfs
7831 array([0.0819612 , 0.44630594, 0.5453811 , 0.57534543, 0.9656205 ])
7832  
7833 Construct the empirical CDF and the K-S statistics (Dn+, Dn-, Dn).
7834  
7835 >>> n = len(x)
7836 >>> ecdfs = np.arange(n+1, dtype=float)/n
7837 >>> cols = np.column_stack([x, ecdfs[1:], cdfs, cdfs - ecdfs[:n],
7838 ... ecdfs[1:] - cdfs])
7839 >>> with np.printoptions(precision=3):
7840 ... print(cols)
7841 [[-1.392 0.2 0.082 0.082 0.118]
7842 [-0.135 0.4 0.446 0.246 -0.046]
7843 [ 0.114 0.6 0.545 0.145 0.055]
7844 [ 0.19 0.8 0.575 -0.025 0.225]
7845 [ 1.82 1. 0.966 0.166 0.034]]
7846 >>> gaps = cols[:, -2:]
7847 >>> Dnpm = np.max(gaps, axis=0)
7848 >>> print(f'Dn-={Dnpm[0]:f}, Dn+={Dnpm[1]:f}')
7849 Dn-=0.246306, Dn+=0.224655
7850 >>> probs = smirnov(n, Dnpm)
7851 >>> print(f'For a sample of size {n} drawn from N(0, 1):',
7852 ... f' Smirnov n={n}: Prob(Dn- >= {Dnpm[0]:f}) = {probs[0]:.4f}',
7853 ... f' Smirnov n={n}: Prob(Dn+ >= {Dnpm[1]:f}) = {probs[1]:.4f}',
7854 ... sep='\n')
7855 For a sample of size 5 drawn from N(0, 1):
7856 Smirnov n=5: Prob(Dn- >= 0.246306) = 0.4711
7857 Smirnov n=5: Prob(Dn+ >= 0.224655) = 0.5245
7858  
7859 Plot the empirical CDF and the standard normal CDF.
7860  
7861 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
7862 >>> plt.step(np.concatenate(([-2.5], x, [2.5])),
7863 ... np.concatenate((ecdfs, [1])),
7864 ... where='post', label='Empirical CDF')
7865 >>> xx = np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, 100)
7866 >>> plt.plot(xx, target.cdf(xx), '--', label='CDF for N(0, 1)')
7867  
7868 Add vertical lines marking Dn+ and Dn-.
7869  
7870 >>> iminus, iplus = np.argmax(gaps, axis=0)
7871 >>> plt.vlines([x[iminus]], ecdfs[iminus], cdfs[iminus], color='r',
7872 ... alpha=0.5, lw=4)
7873 >>> plt.vlines([x[iplus]], cdfs[iplus], ecdfs[iplus+1], color='m',
7874 ... alpha=0.5, lw=4)
7875  
7876 >>> plt.grid(True)
7877 >>> plt.legend(framealpha=1, shadow=True)
7878 >>> plt.show()
7879 """)
7880  
7881 add_newdoc("smirnovi",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
7882 """
7883 smirnovi(n, p, out=None)
7884  
7885 Inverse to `smirnov`
7886  
7887 Returns `d` such that ``smirnov(n, d) == p``, the critical value
7888 corresponding to `p`.
7889  
7890 Parameters
7891 ----------
7892 n : int
7893 Number of samples
7894 p : float array_like
7895 Probability
7896 out : ndarray, optional
7897 Optional output array for the function results
7898  
7899 Returns
7900 -------
7901 scalar or ndarray
7902 The value(s) of smirnovi(n, p), the critical values.
7903  
7904 See Also
7905 --------
7906 smirnov : The Survival Function (SF) for the distribution
7907 scipy.stats.ksone : Provides the functionality as a continuous distribution
7908 kolmogorov, kolmogi : Functions for the two-sided distribution
7909 scipy.stats.kstwobign : Two-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov distribution, large n
7910  
7911 Notes
7912 -----
7913 `smirnov` is used by `stats.kstest` in the application of the
7914 Kolmogorov-Smirnov Goodness of Fit test. For historical reasons this
7915 function is exposed in `scpy.special`, but the recommended way to achieve
7916 the most accurate CDF/SF/PDF/PPF/ISF computations is to use the
7917 `stats.ksone` distribution.
7918  
7919 Examples
7920 --------
7921 >>> from scipy.special import smirnovi, smirnov
7922  
7923 >>> n = 24
7924 >>> deviations = [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]
7925  
7926 Use `smirnov` to compute the complementary CDF of the Smirnov
7927 distribution for the given number of samples and deviations.
7928  
7929 >>> p = smirnov(n, deviations)
7930 >>> p
7931 array([0.58105083, 0.12826832, 0.01032231])
7932  
7933 The inverse function ``smirnovi(n, p)`` returns ``deviations``.
7934  
7935 >>> smirnovi(n, p)
7936 array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
7937

7957 add_newdoc("spence",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
7958 r"""
7959 spence(z, out=None)
7960  
7961 Spence's function, also known as the dilogarithm.
7962  
7963 It is defined to be
7964  
7965 .. math::
7966 \int_1^z \frac{\log(t)}{1 - t}dt
7967  
7968 for complex :math:`z`, where the contour of integration is taken
7969 to avoid the branch cut of the logarithm. Spence's function is
7970 analytic everywhere except the negative real axis where it has a
7971 branch cut.
7972  
7973 Parameters
7974 ----------
7975 z : array_like
7976 Points at which to evaluate Spence's function
7977 out : ndarray, optional
7978 Optional output array for the function results
7979  
7980 Returns
7981 -------
7982 s : scalar or ndarray
7983 Computed values of Spence's function
7984  
7985 Notes
7986 -----
7987 There is a different convention which defines Spence's function by
7988 the integral
7989  
7990 .. math::
7991 -\int_0^z \frac{\log(1 - t)}{t}dt;
7992  
7993 this is our ``spence(1 - z)``.
7994  
7995 Examples
7996 --------
7997 >>> import numpy as np
7998 >>> from scipy.special import spence
7999 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
8000  
8001 The function is defined for complex inputs:
8002  
8003 >>> spence([1-1j, 1.5+2j, 3j, -10-5j])
8004 array([-0.20561676+0.91596559j, -0.86766909-1.39560134j,
8005 -0.59422064-2.49129918j, -1.14044398+6.80075924j])
8006  
8007 For complex inputs on the branch cut, which is the negative real axis,
8008 the function returns the limit for ``z`` with positive imaginary part.
8009 For example, in the following, note the sign change of the imaginary
8010 part of the output for ``z = -2`` and ``z = -2 - 1e-8j``:
8011  
8012 >>> spence([-2 + 1e-8j, -2, -2 - 1e-8j])
8013 array([2.32018041-3.45139229j, 2.32018042-3.4513923j ,
8014 2.32018041+3.45139229j])
8015  
8016 The function returns ``nan`` for real inputs on the branch cut:
8017  
8018 >>> spence(-1.5)
8019 nan
8020  
8021 Verify some particular values: ``spence(0) = pi**2/6``,
8022 ``spence(1) = 0`` and ``spence(2) = -pi**2/12``.
8023  
8024 >>> spence([0, 1, 2])
8025 array([ 1.64493407, 0. , -0.82246703])
8026 >>> np.pi**2/6, -np.pi**2/12
8027 (1.6449340668482264, -0.8224670334241132)
8028  
8029 Verify the identity::
8030  
8031 spence(z) + spence(1 - z) = pi**2/6 - log(z)*log(1 - z)
8032  
8033 >>> z = 3 + 4j
8034 >>> spence(z) + spence(1 - z)
8035 (-2.6523186143876067+1.8853470951513935j)
8036 >>> np.pi**2/6 - np.log(z)*np.log(1 - z)
8037 (-2.652318614387606+1.885347095151394j)
8038  
8039 Plot the function for positive real input.
8040  
8041 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
8042 >>> x = np.linspace(0, 6, 400)
8043 >>> ax.plot(x, spence(x))
8044 >>> ax.grid()
8045 >>> ax.set_xlabel('x')
8046 >>> ax.set_title('spence(x)')
8047 >>> plt.show()
8048 """)

8050 add_newdoc(
8051 "stdtr",
8052 r"""
8053 stdtr(df, t, out=None)
8054  
8055 Student t distribution cumulative distribution function
8056  
8057 Returns the integral:
8058  
8059 .. math::
8060 \frac{\Gamma((df+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi df} \Gamma(df/2)}
8061 \int_{-\infty}^t (1+x^2/df)^{-(df+1)/2}\, dx
8062  
8063 Parameters
8064 ----------
8065 df : array_like
8066 Degrees of freedom
8067 t : array_like
8068 Upper bound of the integral
8069 out : ndarray, optional
8070 Optional output array for the function results
8071  
8072 Returns
8073 -------
8074 scalar or ndarray
8075 Value of the Student t CDF at t
8076  
8077 See Also
8078 --------
8079 stdtridf : inverse of stdtr with respect to `df`
8080 stdtrit : inverse of stdtr with respect to `t`
8081 scipy.stats.t : student t distribution
8082  
8083 Notes
8084 -----
8085 The student t distribution is also available as `scipy.stats.t`.
8086 Calling `stdtr` directly can improve performance compared to the
8087 ``cdf`` method of `scipy.stats.t` (see last example below).
8088  
8089 Examples
8090 --------
8091 Calculate the function for ``df=3`` at ``t=1``.
8092  
8093 >>> import numpy as np
8094 >>> from scipy.special import stdtr
8095 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
8096 >>> stdtr(3, 1)
8097 0.8044988905221148
8098  
8099 Plot the function for three different degrees of freedom.
8100  
8101 >>> x = np.linspace(-10, 10, 1000)
8102 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
8103 >>> parameters = [(1, "solid"), (3, "dashed"), (10, "dotted")]
8104 >>> for (df, linestyle) in parameters:
8105 ... ax.plot(x, stdtr(df, x), ls=linestyle, label=f"$df={df}$")
8106 >>> ax.legend()
8107 >>> ax.set_title("Student t distribution cumulative distribution function")
8108 >>> plt.show()
8109  
8110 The function can be computed for several degrees of freedom at the same
8111 time by providing a NumPy array or list for `df`:
8112  
8113 >>> stdtr([1, 2, 3], 1)
8114 array([0.75 , 0.78867513, 0.80449889])
8115  
8116 It is possible to calculate the function at several points for several
8117 different degrees of freedom simultaneously by providing arrays for `df`
8118 and `t` with shapes compatible for broadcasting. Compute `stdtr` at
8119 4 points for 3 degrees of freedom resulting in an array of shape 3x4.
8120  
8121 >>> dfs = np.array([[1], [2], [3]])
8122 >>> t = np.array([2, 4, 6, 8])
8123 >>> dfs.shape, t.shape
8124 ((3, 1), (4,))
8125  
8126 >>> stdtr(dfs, t)
8127 array([[0.85241638, 0.92202087, 0.94743154, 0.96041658],
8128 [0.90824829, 0.97140452, 0.98666426, 0.99236596],
8129 [0.93033702, 0.98599577, 0.99536364, 0.99796171]])
8130  
8131 The t distribution is also available as `scipy.stats.t`. Calling `stdtr`
8132 directly can be much faster than calling the ``cdf`` method of
8133 `scipy.stats.t`. To get the same results, one must use the following
8134 parametrization: ``scipy.stats.t(df).cdf(x) = stdtr(df, x)``.
8135  
8136 >>> from scipy.stats import t
8137 >>> df, x = 3, 1
8138 >>> stdtr_result = stdtr(df, x) # this can be faster than below
8139 >>> stats_result = t(df).cdf(x)
8140 >>> stats_result == stdtr_result # test that results are equal
8141 True
8142 """)
8143  
8144 add_newdoc("stdtridf",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
8145 """
8146 stdtridf(p, t, out=None)
8147  
8148 Inverse of `stdtr` vs df
8149  
8150 Returns the argument df such that stdtr(df, t) is equal to `p`.
8151  
8152 Parameters
8153 ----------
8154 p : array_like
8155 Probability
8156 t : array_like
8157 Upper bound of the integral
8158 out : ndarray, optional
8159 Optional output array for the function results
8160  
8161 Returns
8162 -------
8163 df : scalar or ndarray
8164 Value of `df` such that ``stdtr(df, t) == p``
8165  
8166 See Also
8167 --------
8168 stdtr : Student t CDF
8169 stdtrit : inverse of stdtr with respect to `t`
8170 scipy.stats.t : Student t distribution
8171  
8172 Examples
8173 --------
8174 Compute the student t cumulative distribution function for one
8175 parameter set.
8176  
8177 >>> from scipy.special import stdtr, stdtridf
8178 >>> df, x = 5, 2
8179 >>> cdf_value = stdtr(df, x)
8180 >>> cdf_value
8181 0.9490302605850709
8182  
8183 Verify that `stdtridf` recovers the original value for `df` given
8184 the CDF value and `x`.
8185  
8186 >>> stdtridf(cdf_value, x)
8187 5.0
8188 """)
8189  
8190 add_newdoc("stdtrit",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
8191 """
8192 stdtrit(df, p, out=None)
8193  
8194 The `p`-th quantile of the student t distribution.
8195  
8196 This function is the inverse of the student t distribution cumulative
8197 distribution function (CDF), returning `t` such that `stdtr(df, t) = p`.
8198  
8199 Returns the argument `t` such that stdtr(df, t) is equal to `p`.
8200  
8201 Parameters
8202 ----------
8203 df : array_like
8204 Degrees of freedom
8205 p : array_like
8206 Probability
8207 out : ndarray, optional
8208 Optional output array for the function results
8209  
8210 Returns
8211 -------
8212 t : scalar or ndarray
8213 Value of `t` such that ``stdtr(df, t) == p``
8214  
8215 See Also
8216 --------
8217 stdtr : Student t CDF
8218 stdtridf : inverse of stdtr with respect to `df`
8219 scipy.stats.t : Student t distribution
8220  
8221 Notes
8222 -----
8223 The student t distribution is also available as `scipy.stats.t`. Calling
8224 `stdtrit` directly can improve performance compared to the ``ppf``
8225 method of `scipy.stats.t` (see last example below).
8226  
8227 Examples
8228 --------
8229 `stdtrit` represents the inverse of the student t distribution CDF which
8230 is available as `stdtr`. Here, we calculate the CDF for ``df`` at
8231 ``x=1``. `stdtrit` then returns ``1`` up to floating point errors
8232 given the same value for `df` and the computed CDF value.
8233  
8234 >>> import numpy as np
8235 >>> from scipy.special import stdtr, stdtrit
8236 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
8237 >>> df = 3
8238 >>> x = 1
8239 >>> cdf_value = stdtr(df, x)
8240 >>> stdtrit(df, cdf_value)
8241 0.9999999994418539
8242  
8243 Plot the function for three different degrees of freedom.
8244  
8245 >>> x = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)
8246 >>> parameters = [(1, "solid"), (2, "dashed"), (5, "dotted")]
8247 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
8248 >>> for (df, linestyle) in parameters:
8249 ... ax.plot(x, stdtrit(df, x), ls=linestyle, label=f"$df={df}$")
8250 >>> ax.legend()
8251 >>> ax.set_ylim(-10, 10)
8252 >>> ax.set_title("Student t distribution quantile function")
8253 >>> plt.show()
8254  
8255 The function can be computed for several degrees of freedom at the same
8256 time by providing a NumPy array or list for `df`:
8257  
8258 >>> stdtrit([1, 2, 3], 0.7)
8259 array([0.72654253, 0.6172134 , 0.58438973])
8260  
8261 It is possible to calculate the function at several points for several
8262 different degrees of freedom simultaneously by providing arrays for `df`
8263 and `p` with shapes compatible for broadcasting. Compute `stdtrit` at
8264 4 points for 3 degrees of freedom resulting in an array of shape 3x4.
8265  
8266 >>> dfs = np.array([[1], [2], [3]])
8267 >>> p = np.array([0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 0.8])
8268 >>> dfs.shape, p.shape
8269 ((3, 1), (4,))
8270  
8271 >>> stdtrit(dfs, p)
8272 array([[-1.37638192, -0.3249197 , 0.72654253, 1.37638192],
8273 [-1.06066017, -0.28867513, 0.6172134 , 1.06066017],
8274 [-0.97847231, -0.27667066, 0.58438973, 0.97847231]])
8275  
8276 The t distribution is also available as `scipy.stats.t`. Calling `stdtrit`
8277 directly can be much faster than calling the ``ppf`` method of
8278 `scipy.stats.t`. To get the same results, one must use the following
8279 parametrization: ``scipy.stats.t(df).ppf(x) = stdtrit(df, x)``.
8280  
8281 >>> from scipy.stats import t
8282 >>> df, x = 3, 0.5
8283 >>> stdtrit_result = stdtrit(df, x) # this can be faster than below
8284 >>> stats_result = t(df).ppf(x)
8285 >>> stats_result == stdtrit_result # test that results are equal
8286 True
8287 """)
