8289 add_newdoc(
8290 "tklmbda",
8291 r"""
8292 tklmbda(x, lmbda, out=None)
8293  
8294 Cumulative distribution function of the Tukey lambda distribution.
8295  
8296 Parameters
8297 ----------
8298 x, lmbda : array_like
8299 Parameters
8300 out : ndarray, optional
8301 Optional output array for the function results
8302  
8303 Returns
8304 -------
8305 cdf : scalar or ndarray
8306 Value of the Tukey lambda CDF
8307  
8308 See Also
8309 --------
8310 scipy.stats.tukeylambda : Tukey lambda distribution
8311  
8312 Examples
8313 --------
8314 >>> import numpy as np
8315 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
8316 >>> from scipy.special import tklmbda, expit
8317  
8318 Compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the Tukey lambda
8319 distribution at several ``x`` values for `lmbda` = -1.5.
8320  
8321 >>> x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 9)
8322 >>> x
8323 array([-2. , -1.5, -1. , -0.5, 0. , 0.5, 1. , 1.5, 2. ])
8324 >>> tklmbda(x, -1.5)
8325 array([0.34688734, 0.3786554 , 0.41528805, 0.45629737, 0.5 ,
8326 0.54370263, 0.58471195, 0.6213446 , 0.65311266])
8327  
8328 When `lmbda` is 0, the function is the logistic sigmoid function,
8329 which is implemented in `scipy.special` as `expit`.
8330  
8331 >>> tklmbda(x, 0)
8332 array([0.11920292, 0.18242552, 0.26894142, 0.37754067, 0.5 ,
8333 0.62245933, 0.73105858, 0.81757448, 0.88079708])
8334 >>> expit(x)
8335 array([0.11920292, 0.18242552, 0.26894142, 0.37754067, 0.5 ,
8336 0.62245933, 0.73105858, 0.81757448, 0.88079708])
8337  
8338 When `lmbda` is 1, the Tukey lambda distribution is uniform on the
8339 interval [-1, 1], so the CDF increases linearly.
8340  
8341 >>> t = np.linspace(-1, 1, 9)
8342 >>> tklmbda(t, 1)
8343 array([0. , 0.125, 0.25 , 0.375, 0.5 , 0.625, 0.75 , 0.875, 1. ])
8344  
8345 In the following, we generate plots for several values of `lmbda`.
8346  
8347 The first figure shows graphs for `lmbda` <= 0.
8348  
8349 >>> styles = ['-', '-.', '--', ':']
8350 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
8351 >>> x = np.linspace(-12, 12, 500)
8352 >>> for k, lmbda in enumerate([-1.0, -0.5, 0.0]):
8353 ... y = tklmbda(x, lmbda)
8354 ... ax.plot(x, y, styles[k], label=rf'$\lambda$ = {lmbda:-4.1f}')
8355  
8356 >>> ax.set_title(r'tklmbda(x, $\lambda$)')
8357 >>> ax.set_label('x')
8358 >>> ax.legend(framealpha=1, shadow=True)
8359 >>> ax.grid(True)
8360  
8361 The second figure shows graphs for `lmbda` > 0. The dots in the
8362 graphs show the bounds of the support of the distribution.
8363  
8364 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
8365 >>> x = np.linspace(-4.2, 4.2, 500)
8366 >>> lmbdas = [0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5]
8367 >>> for k, lmbda in enumerate(lmbdas):
8368 ... y = tklmbda(x, lmbda)
8369 ... ax.plot(x, y, styles[k], label=fr'$\lambda$ = {lmbda}')
8370  
8371 >>> ax.set_prop_cycle(None)
8372 >>> for lmbda in lmbdas:
8373 ... ax.plot([-1/lmbda, 1/lmbda], [0, 1], '.', ms=8)
8374  
8375 >>> ax.set_title(r'tklmbda(x, $\lambda$)')
8376 >>> ax.set_xlabel('x')
8377 >>> ax.legend(framealpha=1, shadow=True)
8378 >>> ax.grid(True)
8379  
8380 >>> plt.tight_layout()
8381 >>> plt.show()
8382  
8383 The CDF of the Tukey lambda distribution is also implemented as the
8384 ``cdf`` method of `scipy.stats.tukeylambda`. In the following,
8385 ``tukeylambda.cdf(x, -0.5)`` and ``tklmbda(x, -0.5)`` compute the
8386 same values:
8387  
8388 >>> from scipy.stats import tukeylambda
8389 >>> x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 9)
8390  
8391 >>> tukeylambda.cdf(x, -0.5)
8392 array([0.21995157, 0.27093858, 0.33541677, 0.41328161, 0.5 ,
8393 0.58671839, 0.66458323, 0.72906142, 0.78004843])
8394  
8395 >>> tklmbda(x, -0.5)
8396 array([0.21995157, 0.27093858, 0.33541677, 0.41328161, 0.5 ,
8397 0.58671839, 0.66458323, 0.72906142, 0.78004843])
8398  
8399 The implementation in ``tukeylambda`` also provides location and scale
8400 parameters, and other methods such as ``pdf()`` (the probability
8401 density function) and ``ppf()`` (the inverse of the CDF), so for
8402 working with the Tukey lambda distribution, ``tukeylambda`` is more
8403 generally useful. The primary advantage of ``tklmbda`` is that it is
8404 significantly faster than ``tukeylambda.cdf``.
8405 """)

8408 r"""
8409 yn(n, x, out=None)
8410  
8411 Bessel function of the second kind of integer order and real argument.
8412  
8413 Parameters
8414 ----------
8415 n : array_like
8416 Order (integer).
8417 x : array_like
8418 Argument (float).
8419 out : ndarray, optional
8420 Optional output array for the function results
8421  
8422 Returns
8423 -------
8424 Y : scalar or ndarray
8425 Value of the Bessel function, :math:`Y_n(x)`.
8426  
8427 See Also
8428 --------
8429 yv : For real order and real or complex argument.
8430 y0: faster implementation of this function for order 0
8431 y1: faster implementation of this function for order 1
8432  
8433 Notes
8434 -----
8435 Wrapper for the Cephes [1]_ routine `yn`.
8436  
8437 The function is evaluated by forward recurrence on `n`, starting with
8438 values computed by the Cephes routines `y0` and `y1`. If ``n = 0`` or 1,
8439 the routine for `y0` or `y1` is called directly.
8440  
8441 References
8442 ----------
8443 .. [1] Cephes Mathematical Functions Library,
8444 http://www.netlib.org/cephes/
8445  
8446 Examples
8447 --------
8448 Evaluate the function of order 0 at one point.
8449  
8450 >>> from scipy.special import yn
8451 >>> yn(0, 1.)
8452 0.08825696421567697
8453  
8454 Evaluate the function at one point for different orders.
8455  
8456 >>> yn(0, 1.), yn(1, 1.), yn(2, 1.)
8457 (0.08825696421567697, -0.7812128213002888, -1.6506826068162546)
8458  
8459 The evaluation for different orders can be carried out in one call by
8460 providing a list or NumPy array as argument for the `v` parameter:
8461  
8462 >>> yn([0, 1, 2], 1.)
8463 array([ 0.08825696, -0.78121282, -1.65068261])
8464  
8465 Evaluate the function at several points for order 0 by providing an
8466 array for `z`.
8467  
8468 >>> import numpy as np
8469 >>> points = np.array([0.5, 3., 8.])
8470 >>> yn(0, points)
8471 array([-0.44451873, 0.37685001, 0.22352149])
8472  
8473 If `z` is an array, the order parameter `v` must be broadcastable to
8474 the correct shape if different orders shall be computed in one call.
8475 To calculate the orders 0 and 1 for an 1D array:
8476  
8477 >>> orders = np.array([[0], [1]])
8478 >>> orders.shape
8479 (2, 1)
8480  
8481 >>> yn(orders, points)
8482 array([[-0.44451873, 0.37685001, 0.22352149],
8483 [-1.47147239, 0.32467442, -0.15806046]])
8484  
8485 Plot the functions of order 0 to 3 from 0 to 10.
8486  
8487 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
8488 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
8489 >>> x = np.linspace(0., 10., 1000)
8490 >>> for i in range(4):
8491 ... ax.plot(x, yn(i, x), label=f'$Y_{i!r}$')
8492 >>> ax.set_ylim(-3, 1)
8493 >>> ax.legend()
8494 >>> plt.show()
8495 """)

8497 add_newdoc("yv",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
8498 r"""
8499 yv(v, z, out=None)
8500  
8501 Bessel function of the second kind of real order and complex argument.
8502  
8503 Parameters
8504 ----------
8505 v : array_like
8506 Order (float).
8507 z : array_like
8508 Argument (float or complex).
8509 out : ndarray, optional
8510 Optional output array for the function results
8511  
8512 Returns
8513 -------
8514 Y : scalar or ndarray
8515 Value of the Bessel function of the second kind, :math:`Y_v(x)`.
8516  
8517 See Also
8518 --------
8519 yve : :math:`Y_v` with leading exponential behavior stripped off.
8520 y0: faster implementation of this function for order 0
8521 y1: faster implementation of this function for order 1
8522  
8523 Notes
8524 -----
8525 For positive `v` values, the computation is carried out using the
8526 AMOS [1]_ `zbesy` routine, which exploits the connection to the Hankel
8527 Bessel functions :math:`H_v^{(1)}` and :math:`H_v^{(2)}`,
8528  
8529 .. math:: Y_v(z) = \frac{1}{2\imath} (H_v^{(1)} - H_v^{(2)}).
8530  
8531 For negative `v` values the formula,
8532  
8533 .. math:: Y_{-v}(z) = Y_v(z) \cos(\pi v) + J_v(z) \sin(\pi v)
8534  
8535 is used, where :math:`J_v(z)` is the Bessel function of the first kind,
8536 computed using the AMOS routine `zbesj`. Note that the second term is
8537 exactly zero for integer `v`; to improve accuracy the second term is
8538 explicitly omitted for `v` values such that `v = floor(v)`.
8539  
8540 References
8541 ----------
8542 .. [1] Donald E. Amos, "AMOS, A Portable Package for Bessel Functions
8543 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",
8544 http://netlib.org/amos/
8545  
8546 Examples
8547 --------
8548 Evaluate the function of order 0 at one point.
8549  
8550 >>> from scipy.special import yv
8551 >>> yv(0, 1.)
8552 0.088256964215677
8553  
8554 Evaluate the function at one point for different orders.
8555  
8556 >>> yv(0, 1.), yv(1, 1.), yv(1.5, 1.)
8557 (0.088256964215677, -0.7812128213002889, -1.102495575160179)
8558  
8559 The evaluation for different orders can be carried out in one call by
8560 providing a list or NumPy array as argument for the `v` parameter:
8561  
8562 >>> yv([0, 1, 1.5], 1.)
8563 array([ 0.08825696, -0.78121282, -1.10249558])
8564  
8565 Evaluate the function at several points for order 0 by providing an
8566 array for `z`.
8567  
8568 >>> import numpy as np
8569 >>> points = np.array([0.5, 3., 8.])
8570 >>> yv(0, points)
8571 array([-0.44451873, 0.37685001, 0.22352149])
8572  
8573 If `z` is an array, the order parameter `v` must be broadcastable to
8574 the correct shape if different orders shall be computed in one call.
8575 To calculate the orders 0 and 1 for an 1D array:
8576  
8577 >>> orders = np.array([[0], [1]])
8578 >>> orders.shape
8579 (2, 1)
8580  
8581 >>> yv(orders, points)
8582 array([[-0.44451873, 0.37685001, 0.22352149],
8583 [-1.47147239, 0.32467442, -0.15806046]])
8584  
8585 Plot the functions of order 0 to 3 from 0 to 10.
8586  
8587 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
8588 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
8589 >>> x = np.linspace(0., 10., 1000)
8590 >>> for i in range(4):
8591 ... ax.plot(x, yv(i, x), label=f'$Y_{i!r}$')
8592 >>> ax.set_ylim(-3, 1)
8593 >>> ax.legend()
8594 >>> plt.show()
8595  
8596 """)

8598 add_newdoc("yve",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
8599 r"""
8600 yve(v, z, out=None)
8601  
8602 Exponentially scaled Bessel function of the second kind of real order.
8603  
8604 Returns the exponentially scaled Bessel function of the second
8605 kind of real order `v` at complex `z`::
8606  
8607 yve(v, z) = yv(v, z) * exp(-abs(z.imag))
8608  
8609 Parameters
8610 ----------
8611 v : array_like
8612 Order (float).
8613 z : array_like
8614 Argument (float or complex).
8615 out : ndarray, optional
8616 Optional output array for the function results
8617  
8618 Returns
8619 -------
8620 Y : scalar or ndarray
8621 Value of the exponentially scaled Bessel function.
8622  
8623 See Also
8624 --------
8625 yv: Unscaled Bessel function of the second kind of real order.
8626  
8627 Notes
8628 -----
8629 For positive `v` values, the computation is carried out using the
8630 AMOS [1]_ `zbesy` routine, which exploits the connection to the Hankel
8631 Bessel functions :math:`H_v^{(1)}` and :math:`H_v^{(2)}`,
8632  
8633 .. math:: Y_v(z) = \frac{1}{2\imath} (H_v^{(1)} - H_v^{(2)}).
8634  
8635 For negative `v` values the formula,
8636  
8637 .. math:: Y_{-v}(z) = Y_v(z) \cos(\pi v) + J_v(z) \sin(\pi v)
8638  
8639 is used, where :math:`J_v(z)` is the Bessel function of the first kind,
8640 computed using the AMOS routine `zbesj`. Note that the second term is
8641 exactly zero for integer `v`; to improve accuracy the second term is
8642 explicitly omitted for `v` values such that `v = floor(v)`.
8643  
8644 Exponentially scaled Bessel functions are useful for large `z`:
8645 for these, the unscaled Bessel functions can easily under-or overflow.
8646  
8647 References
8648 ----------
8649 .. [1] Donald E. Amos, "AMOS, A Portable Package for Bessel Functions
8650 of a Complex Argument and Nonnegative Order",
8651 http://netlib.org/amos/
8652  
8653 Examples
8654 --------
8655 Compare the output of `yv` and `yve` for large complex arguments for `z`
8656 by computing their values for order ``v=1`` at ``z=1000j``. We see that
8657 `yv` returns nan but `yve` returns a finite number:
8658  
8659 >>> import numpy as np
8660 >>> from scipy.special import yv, yve
8661 >>> v = 1
8662 >>> z = 1000j
8663 >>> yv(v, z), yve(v, z)
8664 ((nan+nanj), (-0.012610930256928629+7.721967686709076e-19j))
8665  
8666 For real arguments for `z`, `yve` returns the same as `yv` up to
8667 floating point errors.
8668  
8669 >>> v, z = 1, 1000
8670 >>> yv(v, z), yve(v, z)
8671 (-0.02478433129235178, -0.02478433129235179)
8672  
8673 The function can be evaluated for several orders at the same time by
8674 providing a list or NumPy array for `v`:
8675  
8676 >>> yve([1, 2, 3], 1j)
8677 array([-0.20791042+0.14096627j, 0.38053618-0.04993878j,
8678 0.00815531-1.66311097j])
8679  
8680 In the same way, the function can be evaluated at several points in one
8681 call by providing a list or NumPy array for `z`:
8682  
8683 >>> yve(1, np.array([1j, 2j, 3j]))
8684 array([-0.20791042+0.14096627j, -0.21526929+0.01205044j,
8685 -0.19682671+0.00127278j])
8686  
8687 It is also possible to evaluate several orders at several points
8688 at the same time by providing arrays for `v` and `z` with
8689 broadcasting compatible shapes. Compute `yve` for two different orders
8690 `v` and three points `z` resulting in a 2x3 array.
8691  
8692 >>> v = np.array([[1], [2]])
8693 >>> z = np.array([3j, 4j, 5j])
8694 >>> v.shape, z.shape
8695 ((2, 1), (3,))
8696  
8697 >>> yve(v, z)
8698 array([[-1.96826713e-01+1.27277544e-03j, -1.78750840e-01+1.45558819e-04j,
8699 -1.63972267e-01+1.73494110e-05j],
8700 [1.94960056e-03-1.11782545e-01j, 2.02902325e-04-1.17626501e-01j,
8701 2.27727687e-05-1.17951906e-01j]])
8702 """)

8784 """
8785 owens_t(h, a, out=None)
8786  
8787 Owen's T Function.
8788  
8789 The function T(h, a) gives the probability of the event
8790 (X > h and 0 < Y < a * X) where X and Y are independent
8791 standard normal random variables.
8792  
8793 Parameters
8794 ----------
8795 h: array_like
8796 Input value.
8797 a: array_like
8798 Input value.
8799 out : ndarray, optional
8800 Optional output array for the function results
8801  
8802 Returns
8803 -------
8804 t: scalar or ndarray
8805 Probability of the event (X > h and 0 < Y < a * X),
8806 where X and Y are independent standard normal random variables.
8807  
8808 References
8809 ----------
8810 .. [1] M. Patefield and D. Tandy, "Fast and accurate calculation of
8811 Owen's T Function", Statistical Software vol. 5, pp. 1-25, 2000.
8812  
8813 Examples
8814 --------
8815 >>> from scipy import special
8816 >>> a = 3.5
8817 >>> h = 0.78
8818 >>> special.owens_t(h, a)
8819 0.10877216734852274

8827 add_newdoc("ndtri_exp",
  • E128 Continuation line under-indented for visual indent
8828 r"""
8829 ndtri_exp(y, out=None)
8830  
8831 Inverse of `log_ndtr` vs x. Allows for greater precision than
8832 `ndtri` composed with `numpy.exp` for very small values of y and for
8833 y close to 0.
8834  
8835 Parameters
8836 ----------
8837 y : array_like of float
8838 Function argument
8839 out : ndarray, optional
8840 Optional output array for the function results
8841  
8842 Returns
8843 -------
8844 scalar or ndarray
8845 Inverse of the log CDF of the standard normal distribution, evaluated
8846 at y.
8847  
8848 See Also
8849 --------
8850 log_ndtr : log of the standard normal cumulative distribution function
8851 ndtr : standard normal cumulative distribution function
8852 ndtri : standard normal percentile function
8853  
8854 Examples
8855 --------
8856 >>> import numpy as np
8857 >>> import scipy.special as sc
8858  
8859 `ndtri_exp` agrees with the naive implementation when the latter does
8860 not suffer from underflow.
8861  
8862 >>> sc.ndtri_exp(-1)
8863 -0.33747496376420244
8864 >>> sc.ndtri(np.exp(-1))
8865 -0.33747496376420244
8866  
8867 For extreme values of y, the naive approach fails
8868  
8869 >>> sc.ndtri(np.exp(-800))
8870 -inf
8871 >>> sc.ndtri(np.exp(-1e-20))
8872 inf
8873  
8874 whereas `ndtri_exp` is still able to compute the result to high precision.
8875  
8876 >>> sc.ndtri_exp(-800)
8877 -39.88469483825668
8878 >>> sc.ndtri_exp(-1e-20)
8879 9.262340089798409
8880 """)
